The Company has purchased from Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, Bart., under the contract hereinafter referred to, the well-known Brewery and Wine and Spirit Businesses hitherto carried on as PETER WALKER & SON and MORRO & CO., at Warrington and Liverpool, A. B. WALKER & SONS, at Burton-on-Trent, and A. B. WALKER & CO., at Liverpool, as well as at Manchester, Salford, Birmingham, Bootle, Birkenhead. Chester, Crewe, Widnes, and elsewhere. The businesses are taken over by the Company as from 31st December, 1889, the profits for theyear 1890 beingapportioned as on the date of the contract, and from that date the Vendor receives interest at £4 per cent., on £2,850,000, the purchase money. or the unpaid portion of it f or•the time being. The Property acquired by the Company comprises the two breweries at Warrington and the breweryat Burton-on-Trent, with a bonded warehouse, offices' stores, and stabling at Liverpool ; also all the fixed and loose plant, rolling stock, horses, casks, and barrels, and the stock of malt, hops, wines, spirits, and beers at the breweries, stores, to., certain trade balances and business loans ; and in addition thereto the Vendor's interest in upwards of 253 freehold, copyhold, and leasehold licensed properties, and a number of shops and dwelling-houses, cottages, and lands adjoining, and the entire goodwill of the businesses as going concerns. Sir Andrew B. Walker. who lathe Chairman of the Board of Directors, retains (by himself and nominees) the Ordinary I Shares, as well as a third of the Mortgage Debentures and Preference Shares • and Mr. Peter Carlaw Walker, Mr. John Reid Walker, :sad 'Mr. William Hall Walker (three sons of Sir Andrew) who have for the last twelve years been associated in the active management, have also joined the Board, Mr. John R. Walker and Mr. William H. Walker being Managing Directors. .

The Books of the businesses have been independently examined by Messrs. Ilarmood Banner 8: Son, of Liverpool, Chartered Accountants, who certify as follows "24, North, John-street. " Liverpool, February 17th, 1890. "We have carefully examined the accounts apper- " talning to the business carried on by Sir Andrew Barclay " Walker, Bart., at Warrington, Burton-on-Trent, Liver- "pool, Manchester, Birkenhead, Chester, and other places. "The sales quoted in excise barrels for the three years "ending 31st December, 1889, are as follows : " For the year 1887 ... 337,773 Barrels. 1888 .. 383,774 „ „ „ 1889 ... 418.282 „ "The average profits during the three years ending "31st December, 1889, have amounted to "£201,277 Bs. 10d, per annum. "The profits for the single year ending 31st Decem- " bar. 1889, have amounted to £210,224 12s. Ild. "In stating these profits, an ample provision his, in "our opinion, been made for all depreciation of property "and plant, extinction of leases or goodwill, and for bad "and doubtful debts; and the accounts have been ad- justed for this purpose where nvessary. "The above profits have been arrived at before any " charge is made in the accounts for personal services of "Vendor or his sobs, or for interest on capital, or income "tax.

HARMOOD BANNER AND-SON§, " Chartered Accountant." With the improvements now being made and • cmitemplated, the output of 418,282 barrels can, it is believed, be considerably increased, but, taking the profits for 1889 at the amount certified by the Accountants Awl deducting the interest on _

The difference between £2,650,000 and the total capital is £150,000, and the assets acquired by the Company, In addi- tion to the properties and businesses, include stocks on hand, and outstanding accounts, amounting to upwards of R,154,0,7:0. The contracts and arrangements for the purchase of properties and for advances upon premises and other contracts referred to In the next paragraph, amount to about £160.090, and the Company will therefore have a considerable surplus available for cash working capital, and the extension and development of the business and other purposes. The trade contracts WA obligations taken over by the Com- pany are of the usual chaeacter, and in addition there are I contracts for alterations and improvements at the breweries, I and at various of the licensed houses and properties ; also for the purchase and leasing of, or for advancing moneys upon further licensed and other premises. It is impracticable to specify these in detail, and applioations will be received only upon the footing that the applicants waive the insertion herein of dates and names of parties to any contract,, and waive compliance with section 33 of the Companies Act, 1667. The contract for the purchase of the businesses and properties made between Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, Bart., of the one part, and the Company of the other part, is dated 17th April, 1890. The above-mentioned contract, the certidcate of Messrs. Harntood Banner ,k Soh, the Trust Deed for securing the Debentures, and copies of the Memorandum and Articles of Association and form of Debenture, can be inspected at the Offices of the Solicitors.

Application will be made for a quotation on the Stock Ex- change in respect of the Debentures and Preference Shares. -Applications for Debentares or Preference Shanes must be made in the accompanying Forms and forwarded to the Bankers, with a remittance for the amount of the deposit. If no allotment is maderthe deposit will be returned in ; and where the amount allotted is less than that applied for the balance will be applied towards the payment due on allot- ment, and any excess returned to the applicant. Failure to pay any instalment when due will render the previous pay- ments liaWe to forfeiture. AN APRIL MOOD. ' Whyfis Cynthia very Mir, In my eyes beyond ? • 'Tis no easy thinz to say, " But I think a reason good Is because in every mood She is like an Anril day. • In an April mood she'll sit While above tier eloudlets flit. And she'll be as sad as they. In an'April mood again. Just like.sunshine after rain, •• Smiles will chase her tears away. Soulless beauty, haughty graze, Lend no charm to any face Such as Cynthia's has for me. This it is that makes her fair. In my eyes beyond compare: • Ever-ready sympathy! —C,assen Magazine.

_-- - - - Every man desires to live lonz ; but no man would be

old. - • Nothing is more dangerous than a friend without dis- cretion; even a prudent enemy is preferable. Advice, like snow, the softer it falls, the longer it dwells upon, and the deeper it sinks into, the mind. "Father, they tell us about the angry ocean. What makes the ocean angry ?" "Oh, it has been crossed so often." The greatest friend of truth is time, her greatest enemy is prejudice, and her constant companion is humility. Caller: "Has your daughter's married life so far proved a happy one." Mrs. Vernon: " Very ; her husband, you know, is a commercial traveller." Happy is the man who can comfort himself with hav- ing employed any one day of his life so perfectly well as he might and ought to have done. Virtue can never be attained without great pains and diligence; and if you cool and linger in this pursuit the moment that you gain not ground you lose it. Industry is essentially sociaL No man can improve himself or his neighbours without neiehbourly help; I and to better the world is to set the world to work to- gether. Let grace and goodness be the principal loadstone of thy affections; for love which bath ends will have an end, whereas that which is founded on true virtue will always continue. The greatest of fools is he that imposes on himself, and in his greatest concern thinks certainly he knows that which he has least studied, and of which he is most profoundedly ignorant Censure and criticism never hurt anybody. If false, they cannot harm you, unless you are wanting in char- acter; and, if true, they show a roan his weak points, , and forewarn him against failure and trouble. Enamoured Swain: "For you, darling, wad lay me doon and dee.' Practical Maid-n: "That sort of thing is quite out of date, Willie. What a girl wants nowa- days is a man who is willing to get up aud hustle for her." Guinevere fat a fancy ball): "Oh, Bann, excuse me, but do take off that terrible nose you have one' Baron Bolero: "It would give me the greatest pleasure to do so. niadame ; but, unfortunately, it is my own—and my only one !" Collapse of Guinevere. Swear !—Precocious Infant: "I think grammar's very cloy, mother. I know all about singler and purest." Proud Mamma: "Do you, dear? That's very clever! Perhaps you can tell me the plural of 'sugar?'" Pre- cocious Infant, after reflection: "Why, lumps, of coupe !" A cute American suggests, as an efficacious mode to discover the difference between a mushroom and a toadstool "to eat it" If you live, it's a mushroom; if von die it's a toadstool. This method may possess the 'merit of originality, but it will not bear the test of experience. The officer on duty for the week gives Instructions to his orderly, whose business it Is to wait at table: "Be- fore removing the soup-plates always ask each person if he would like any more." "Very good, Er." Next day the orderly, respectfully bowing to one of the guests. inquires: "Would the gentlemanlike some more soup?" "Yes, please." "There isn't any left." A thief went into the hall of a Brighton hotel, and gathered up all the hats. He was making his way out, when a visitor came in, and asked him whet he was about. "Ott," says the thief, " taking the gentle- mee'e hats round the corner, to get them blocked." " Well," replied the visitor, "take my hat, too." "Certainly, sir," said the accommodating thief, and vanished. A good story is told of Mr. Howarth, IL?,, the author of a very voluminous work on the Mongols. A lady, on being introduced to him, at once turned the conversation on to dogs, and to put so many questions to him that Mr. Howorth was at last fain to declare that he knew nothing about them; on which his fair interlocutor promptly remarked, "Why, I thought you had written a history of the mongrels!" Loquacious Stranger (driving past the foot of a moun- tain. to driver): "Anything remarkable about this mountain ?" Driver: "There is nothing peculiar about -the hill itself, but there's a queer story connected with it" Stranger: "What is that?" Driver: A young lady and gentleman went out for a walk on this hill; they ascended higher and higher, and—never came back again." Stranger: "Dear me! what, then, became of the unhappy pair?" Driver: "They went down on the other side." "One night," says Mr. Grossmith, in "A Society Clown." "there was a breakdown on the railway line, and my father and myself did not arrive in the town until twenty past eight, although we should have com- menced at eight punctually. We dressed in the cab, which flew along like a fire engine. Suddenly we espied a building lighted up, and a large crowd coming out. My father pushed his head out of the window and shouted frantically to the crowd: 'Go back! Go back! It's all right. Grossmith is here. We have arrived. Go back!' Unfortunately it was not our audience, but a congregation leaving a Methodist chapeL" KEEPING A SECRET.—An old soldier tells this story of Stonewall Jackson :—lt was during his valley campaign, and a battle was expected within a day or two, though Jackson's plans were so carefully guarded that not even his adjutant could guess them intelligently. This self- reliance was characteristic of Jackson, and his aversion to telling his plans was well-known among his officers and men. In fact, it was his policy to surprise his own men no less than to surprise the enemy. General Jack- son was one of a group of officers. and another of the group was a Georgia colonel who is still living. Conver- sation was dragging. Jackson was thoughtful and had little to say, and the effect was dampening. Finally, just to revive the conversation, the Georgia Colonel asked abruptly, "General, will we have a fight to- morrow ?" Everybody knew in an instant that the blunder was irreparable, and nobody realised this more than the colonel. Jackson turned quickly and stared full in the speaker's face. Then he slowly surveyed the colonel from head to foot, and back again. The silence was painful. "Colonel," said the general, slowly. but not in ' an unkind tone, "can you keep a secret?" "Yes, general," was the warm, if embarrassed assurance. " know I can, general. Yes, sir —" "Are you quite certain, colonel ?" "I am quite certain, general." "Well, colonel," in the same quiet, even tone, "so can I, sir." The colonel's face flushed crimson, and there was a deathly silence for half a minute or more. "Now," colonel," said Jackson, with some feeling, "that rude- nees of mine hurt me as much as it did you, but I trust that it has taught you a valuable lesson. If we do have a fight to-morrow, colonel, your regiment shall have a Chance." Feattietreirrerie NICENAIIES.—If an epithet is apt and VOoa humoured, even though it may not be precisely complimentary, it will be sure to meet with the patron- age by one or other of the sections of the House. No scruple is felt, for instance, in alluding to a certain prominent member of Lord Salisbury's Government as "Old Morality," or to the Marquess of Granby, who sits in the House as tile representative of a Leicester- shire division, as "Salisbury's Manners." He was formerly Lord Salisbury's private secretary, a gentle- man of remarkable courtesy and affability of demeanour, and by name Mr. Henry Manners. The sobriquet is therefore a humorous play on the name in a double sense, and is just such a one as Parliamentary men seize upon. The "Grand Old Man" has become a familiar appellation both with those who use it derisively and those who express their real and fervent admiration by it. But they are even fonder of a designation which cannot be termed a nickname, but is more properly to be called a pet name. "Randy" is :one of that kind. and would probably cling to the owner of it even though one of these days he should find a seat and a more dignified appellation in the Upper Chamber. "Tay Pay" is another, by which Mr. T. P. O'Connor, the member for the Scotland division of Liverpool, is familiarly known among a large section of the House, just as Mr. Timothy Healy is usually referred to as "Tim," Mr. Matthew Harris is known as "Matt," and Mr. Robert Threshie Reid, Q.C., the Liberal member for Dumfries, is familiarly styled "Bob." Everybody knows who would be meant by "Joe" in the present House of Commons; but there was once an "Old Joe," a more appreciative' and affec- tionate term applied to Mr. Joseph Brotherton, who had been long enough in he House to know all its ins and oats, and whose amiable energy was always at the service of everybody who needed him. Lord Pelmerston was similarly spoken of habitually as "Old Pane" though he also had for many years in the early part of his career the familiar title of "Cupid." In his early days he had a round, cherubic sort of face, and a smart, dapper appearance, that suggested the name, and rendered it so appropriate as to stick to him. Talking Of Sobriquets suggestive by personal appearance, perhaps the cruellest one ever invented was that applied to Lord John Russell when he first went to the Treasury bench. Lord John Russell was very diminutive in person—short and small; and when he was "cast into the Treasury" they dubbed him the "Widow's Mite." Among those who have won for themselves something in the nature of a nickname in Parliament is Mr. O'Flanlon, represent a- tive of one of the divisions of Cavan. Mr. O'Hanlan is most assiduous in his practice of making notes of what transpires in the House, and most members know him as "The Recorder."—C'assell's Saturday Journal.

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
A curious rumour is contradicted in" The Court Circular" which says: "We understand there is no truth in the statement that the Queen has the nniform of her German Regiment."

The Queen is expected to remain about a for:- night longer upon the Continent. On quitting Darmstadt, after visiting the Grand Duke of Hess, she returns to Windsor Castle. Iler Majesty pro- ceeds next month to Balmoral.

Verdi, the composer, Ii as secured from the Italian Minister of Public Instruction an edict forbidding the owners of hand organs to play fragments from his operas in public since they pay him no copyright.

It is stated that Madame Patti is taking legal pro- ceedings to restrain an enterprising showman from giving second-hand "Patti concerts" by means of a phonograph, with which, at the San Francisco opera performance,he obtained some capital impres- sions of her voice.

A. paper in Jassy learns from St. Petershurg that the Grand Duke Constantine, cousin of the Czar, was arrested because he composed and published a revo- lutionary poem. The Grand Duke is married to a Princess of Saxe-Alten-burg, and has been in a simi- lar scrape once before.

A private letter received in London on Tuesday from Mr. Schnadhorst announces his recovery of strength and health. He writes from Kimberley, South Africa, where be has been spending some months. He is now so won that he has made arrangements to return home in the middle of next month, and will resume his dutids in Parliammt- street.

The "Daily News" says :—Landlords and tenants vie with each other in denouncing and repudiating the Land Purchase Bill, while it has not been sup- ported by any respectable authority, financial or political. Another warning voice was raised on , Saturday by the "Economist," which pointed out in a powerful article that the alleged sureties were shams.

Madame Thayer, a daughter of General Bertran4, died recently, leaving to 'Prince Napolton a great number of souvenirs of the Emperor Napoleon I. Among them are the red velvet robe which Napoleon wore on grand occasions, the saddle and holsters used by him at Austerlitz, the scarf which he wore at the battle of the Pyramids, and the linen, the pillow-cases, and handkerchiefs from his deathbed.

Jeanne Andre, a Parisian stage beauty four years ago, has just died of paralysis at the Saint Anne's madhouse. A Paris correspondent tells us that she had an imperious temper, inordinate ambition, and passed rapidly from extremes of sanguine hope to deep depression. Her madness first showed itself three years ago in an offer which she made to a jeweller in the Rue de la Paix to buy the whole con- tents of his shop.

Lord Granville has undertaken to preside at the eighth Congress of the Society of French Professors in England, which will be held at Harrow next Monday. It is the custom of the chairman at these gather:ngs to deliver his address in French. This will be an easy task for Lord Granville, who, if it were possible to express himself more gracefully in any language than he does in his own, would cer- tainly do so in French.

" M.A. Cantab" writes: Mr. Chamberlain said at Birmingham last night (April 10), "Sydney Smith said the Puritans hated hear baiting, not because it gave pain to the bear, but because it gave pleasure to the spectators? Macaulay says this early in his second chapter—p. 161 of the Bvo edition—but I 4o not remember it anywhere in Sydney Smith, and believe it belongs to Macaulay. Mr. Chamberlain seems careless and inaccurate in little things and big things alike.

The weekly discussions at the National Liberal Club are introducing the novel.feature of feminine speakers and feminine audience in clubs. On Tues- day night Miss Colenso told the story of Dinizulu's wrongs to an intensely interested audience, and though the narrative was plain in the extreme, it created a very profound impression.. It was the more effective as the speaker so plainly felt what she was saying, and the little pauses she made now and then, in sheer emotion, were more touching than the finest rhetoric. A very strong—indeed an unanswerable—case for inquiry was made out.

The present Lord Normandy is the first instance on record of a sacerdotal marquis in the House of Lords, says the '• World." The late Lord Carlisle, who was a clergyman, was an earl, and so was Lord Abergavenny's father. Lord Ifulgrave (now Lord Normandy) is a popular and hardwerking parish priest, and is greatly beloved at Worsley, a popu- lous district near Manchester, where the living is in the gift of Lord Ellesmere, who presented it some time ago to his brother-in-law. His health is very delicate, and he has been compelled of late to win- ter annually abroad. He generally makes San Remo his he tdquarters, and his ministrations at one of the English churches there have been warmly appreciated by his compatriots, for Lord Normandy is a preacher of no mean capacity.

Countess Tolstoi is a busy woman, for not only does she attend to her domestic concerns, which, with a large family and inefficient Russian ser- vants demand both time and labour, but also to her husband's business affairs. She has, in addi- tion to all this, made numerous hektograph copies I of some of his books that are forbid&u publication, but that in this form are circulated through the mails. Her children are taught to make themselves useful and assist in domestic work. Nine of them are now living, the youngest being a child of two years. The oldest daughter at home, a sweet girl of eighteen, with a pretty, spiritual face, is in ardent sympathy with her tether's views, and often helps him in his labours for and with the poor. All members of this interesting family speak English perfectly.

Mr. Stead, in a very strong number Of the "Review of Reviews," devotes the character sketch to Bismarck. Incidentally he tells a new and interesting story which serves as a kind of key to Bismarck's career :—Prince Bismarck was one (lay passing through the Royal palace at Berlin, when he entered a room in which the young princes were merrily romping and dancing to the music of a barrel organ. The youngsters insisted that Prince Bismarck should stay and dance with them. " I am too old," said the stiff and stately septuagenarian, "and really I cannot dance; but if the Crown Prince will dance, I will grind the organ." The bargain was at once struck. The Crown Prince joined his two brothers, and Prince Bismarck ground away merrily at the organ while the children danced on in high glee. In the midst of their mirth the door opened, and the Kaiser entered. He smiled to see the redoubtable Reichskanzler grinding the barrel organ, and after a word of greeting to his sons he observed,in mock displeasure,to Prince Bismarck, "You begin in good time to make the Heir-Apparent dance to your piping. Why, this is the fourth generation of Hohenzollerns to whom you devote yourself I"

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 19, IP9O.

I do not know whether Prince Albert Victor is to marry Princess Victoria of Teck, but I am tired of reading paragraphs about their impending betrothal. Princess Victoria is no more "Royal" by birth than are Prince Henry of Batteuberg, the Duke of Fife' or Lord Lorne.

Mr. Stead and Mr. "Tit-Bit • Newnes, M.P., have parted company over "The Review of Reviews." Some idea of thzi success which has in four months attended the venture may be formed from the statement that, in the accounting which took place before Mr. Stead paid out his partner. he copyright we- valued at a sum in the neighbourhood of £lO,OOO.

I hoar of a remarkable romance. A woman, lately a convict, has married the chaplain of one of the home county gaols. The clergyman in question was a widower with a large family, and the wedding only became known through an official of the penal department complaining that the wife had not re- ported herself on the ticket of leave. In consequence of the fact coming out, the clergyman has asked for and been appointed to another prison in the North of England.

• There is a capital story about the late Mr. Big- gar, told by a friend of his now in Australia. Try- ing to steal an hour from a much-needed and well- earned rest to give to d,votion, he, despite himself, fell asleep while attending the service of Benediction at one of the Catholic churches in London. The service had ended, and almost all the congregation had departed, when Mr. Biggar awoke. Seeing the benches almost empty, and forgetting where lie was, he sprung to his feet and exclaimed " Mr. Speaker, I move that the house be counted."

A discovery has bez,•n made which shows that the love of our ancestors for drinks spiced with cinna- mon was fully justified. What were not the Dutch ready to do to procure cinnamon and other spices for their mulled wines, and what wonders of navi- gation did they not accomplish in their lumbering vessels in order to till the spice-boxes of their housewives? According to a Paris Correspon- nent, Dr. Charriberland, M. Pasteur's chief assistant, has just discovered that cinnamon is fatal to the typhoid microbe, which must infest the sluggish waters of the Netherlands. ••••••0

Sir William Jenner has not purchased a place near Southampton, but intends to reside principally on his estate near Bishop's Waltham, which he has owned for several years past. Sir William has prac- tically retired from active work for some time, as he has latterly been attending only old patients under special circumstances, and he will continue to do so, and will also visit the Queen as usual. Sir William has for several years been the only physician whom her Majesty has personally consulted, and he has a general charge of her health in conjunction with Dr. James Reid, her resident medical attendant, who has accompanied her to the Continent.

Whatever be the case in England, cremation is making way in France. Sir Spencer Wells, one of cremation's greatest advocates, visiting the new crematorium at Pere la Chaise, found that more than one thousand two hundred unclaimed bodies of persons who have died in the hospitals have been burned. The bodies of three hundred persons belonging to the upper classes have also been cre- mated in compliance with their own nquest, or at the reqaest of their families. Since the beginning of this year there have been thirty-eight eremations of bodies belonging to the well-to-do elass. As an adjunct to the cremation, halls for the temporary deposition of bodies are about to be erected in all the cemeteries similar to those existing in Germany.

Mr. Freeston was anew arrival in Warrington, but in the name of the members of the society he heartily welcomed him. He trusted that the next session would not be very far ad- vanced before he gave them another paper on another poet or 'upon some other subject which he ,foutia most congenial. He (Mr. Davies) should turn to the volumes he possessed of Browning with very- much more zest. div.head: RURAL. SANITARY AUTHORITY'S DISTRICT.
div.p: THE RURAL. SANITARY AUTHORITY'S DISTRICT.

• BY ONE OF OUR STAFF. The sanitary defects of unmade streets aiid wet and sloppy back passages, which were lately brought under the notice of the public in these columns, are by no means confined to those parts of Warrington under the control of the Corporation. There are, in various directions just outside the boundaries of the borough, Several streets of houses, mostly of recent coustruetion, which are under.the jurisdiction of the Warrington Rural Sanitary Auth- ority. For those who are not thoiroughly versed in local boundaries it would•in some directions be next . .

to impossible to determine where the borough ended add where the rural district bigan. Assuming that &person had no positive knowledge as to boundaries, perhaps one of the best methodd of finding out whether he was standing in a locality under the jurisdiction of the Corporation or that of the Rtiral Sanitary Authority would be the sanitary test. In the borough itself the; e is a constant, but, it is to be admitted, a sluggish and inadequate- attempt to wipe off the large arrears of unmade streets; in the Rural. Sanitary Authority's district this attempt does not seem to have been made at all, or if made, it is to such an infinitesimal ex- tent as to be scarcely p ,rceptible. If the person referred to found himself in a back lane where his 'olfactory organs were strongly assailed with disagreeable odours from old-fashioned ashpits, pretty well filled with the festering materials which generally find their way into these recepta- cles, he might safely conclude that he was in a locality that owned the sway of the Rural Sanitary Authority. The venerable ash-midden has long been cmdernned as a pernicious source of disease in thickly inhabited districts, aud a vigorous war- fare has been urged against it within the borough, but just outside the borough line it is still per- mitted to exist by the rural authority. The sani- tary test is an infallible guide to one's whereabouts in the neighbourhood of Warburton-at., off Winwick road, for at the back of this street every house seems to be provided with a fairly capacious ash- midden, and ash-middens are not difficult to find in other back-lanes in this locality. " How often are these ash-pits emptied?" the writer of this article inquired of a house-wife standing at her back gate. "Oh, I couldn't tell you; not often," was the reply. "Once a week ?" " Oh no, nor once a month either." "Perhaps they do not begin to empty them till they are full " That's about it," was the reply. That the ashpits are emptied occasionally was evident from the condition of some of t'se back-lanes into which the stuff was evidently pitched prior to being wheeled away. These back-lanes, being unpaved, are during a considerable part of the year, in a wet and sloppy condition, and it may be easily imagined how thoroughly saturated with unwholesome fluids they will become in the ccurse of time by midden emptying. The streets off Winwick-road are not the only ones OR the outskirts of Warrington, and under the government of the Rural Sanitary Autho- rity, where we find the ashpit. The same primitive contrivances exist at the back of streetta off Liver- pool-road, and it is possible they may be discovered in some other places just without the confines of the borough. It should be added that the back-lanes off Liverpool-road, into which the middens are em- ptied, are paved, but on a recent visit there, I found that the "cleaning up" of the refuse seemed to have been done so hastily or carelessly, as to -make it prudent to piak one's, way along ins rather gingerly fashion, while the smells which pervaded some parts of the narrow passages were by no means of a pleasing character. It has sometimes been said that the reason why the Rural Sanitary Authority is so dilatory iii the matter of astreet paving is that for years past the question of an extension of the borough has been pending. But this seems to be rather an excuse than a reason. It can hardly% be argued that the Corporation would prefer to take over a large number of muddy unmade streets rather than streets which have been properly formed and paved. But apart from this, one might naturally have thought that the first care of a " Sanitary " Authority, even though itc,be a "Rural ^ Sanitary Autticirity, would have beeti for the good sanitation of the district under its charge, and that it would not have been deterred from carrying out its proper duties by vague speculations as to the brae when the borough bouadariea were to be extended.

div.head: WARRINGTON LITERA.RY AND PHILO-
div.p: WARRINGTON LITERA.RY AND PHILO-
SOPHICAL SOCIETY.
THE ANN UAL MEETING.

The annnal meeting of the members of this society was held in the Museum Lecture Room on Tuesday evening, the President, the Rev. H. Gibson Smith, -M.A., in the chair. There was a large attendance. Tne PEESIDENT,IO reviewing the work of the sersion, said that death had removed a former president anti distinguished member in the person of Mr. Bleckly, and more lately they had had to record the loss of Councillor Greening, who was also a faithful friend and supporter of that society. ELECTION OF OFFICERS, &C.

Mr. C. S BURGESS proposed that the following gentle- men constitute the Council for the coming session : President, Mr. F. Monks—(appld.use)—vice-president, the Rev. H. Gibson Smith; Council, Messrs. Robert Davies, John Dun (hon treasurer), Charles White, Win. Owen, W. D. Jeans, J. D. Buckton, and J. Rymer Young (hon. secretary.)—Mr. ALFRED JOLLEY seconded the motion, which was agreed to.
THE It-ETIRING PRESIDENT.

Mr. ROBERT Dsviss proposed a vote of thanks to the retiring president, the Rev. H. G. Smith, for the valuable services which had bee's rendered by him during the past session, and who, he said, had given himself a world of pains to choose subjects which he had thought would be congenial to-all of them. So faras he(Mr.Davies)was cot- cerned, he respected mental activity, in whatever depart- ment it was found. He was also very much in favour of bodily activity ; at the same time, he should prefer to see that assembly, which was the representative of themental activity of Warrington, better supported by the gentle- men of the town. (Hear, hear.) Those who had favoured them with papers had given them their time and intellee. and they were thankful to them for it, and it would be a want of respect on the pars of the members if they ab- stained from attending these meetings •, that was of course, unless they Were prevented by other and more pressing engagements. He was sure that all present would approve of the proposition he was now submitting to the meeting, as well as of the selection of Mr. Fredk. Monks as president of the society for the ensuing session. (Applause.) Several of them consulted. together before the meeting commenced, and the Council unanimously came to the conclusion that a gentleman who had been so regular in his attendance, and who had been so many years a supporter of the society as Mr. Monks had been, must regard it as a kind of duty to undertake the office of president for the ensuing year. He was pleases; to hear that the choice of the Council had been ratified by the unanimous vote of the }meeting. (Applause.) He had much pleasure in proposing a vote of thanks to the retiring president. (Applause).—Mr. SBITH seconded the motion which was put to the meeting and unanimously agreed to.

div.head: MMIABERS IN ARREARS.
div.p: MMIABERS IN ARREARS.

The FloN. SECRETARY observed that a considerable number of members of the society had not yet paid their subscriptions. The society had already had notice that their liabilities were to be increased, as they would have to pay an additional rent for the use of the room in which they were then assembled, and as their income, even when all their subscriptions were paid, was only about sufficient to meet their expenses, the audience would readily understand how matters would be facili- tated if they had a balance in hand. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) PAYER ON ROBERT BROWNING. A paperqra •• Robert Browning : teacher and poet," was then read by the Rev. F. K. Free,ston. In the course of it Mr Freeston said that the death of the poet had directed upon him a general attention not readily ac- corded firm during life. From first to last he was admired by the few, ignored or derided by the many. Among the many his name was little better than a by-word for obscurity, his fame discussed and dismissed at dinner party dialogues. "Do you like Browning ?" "No ; I don't Understand him." Chorus tof guests, "Nobody does, not even hitnaelf." Verdict, nem. con." Browning 's a fraud; pass the \sup." (Laughter and applause.) He (Mr. Preeston) put forward a plea for the more serious study of his work by the members of that literary and philo- sophical society. It. was charged against Browning that he was guilty of rough, harsh, ungrammatical, and dark doings ; that his writings were either forests of pure be- wilderment or deserts of waste cammonplace; that he had perpetrated some of the strangest vagaries ever thrust upon an uuwilling world in the shape of verse; that his metre, was jagged and his rhyme grotesque, his verbosity painful, lits prolixity unendurable, his motive inconceiv- able, andgib meaning incomprehensible. That was a rather lies t indictment, ridiculous if false and made by a feWt;' serious if true and* representing the many. There was: a temperate criticism of Browning„ a just a;ppreciation of his powen, a due admission of his limitations, which would ultimately win from the world his 'need," and which to-day ought to save us from hasty rejection on the one hand and uncritical adulatioa-en the other. BY GRORGB HULL.

"Well," said Bill, "id were Torn Langton as wet tellin' mo. fle'd ridden vri' Dais when he war gooin' to a fair somewheer near Wigan, an' laughed welly calf way gooin'; for Dan lied bin quite th' lively side eawt. They stopped somewheer o'er gooin' wheer th' tickets bed to be collected, an' a bit afoot they reyched th' place Dan towd Toni as he meant herrn' a' lark ' wi' th' collector. Tom said, • Tha'd better led id alooan, Dan; they're dangerous fooak to play tricks on are these railway chaps. They're te' sharp for thee.' " "Well," said Dan, "aw.rn not aboon hofe theer,' as they say, sometimes; but aw'll warrant aw'm sharper than one or two chaps as they hey at this next station." "An' wod are to beawn to do, like?" Torn axed him. " Tha sees these two cards," said Dan. "Aye," said Tom. " Well, one's mi gradely railway ticket —paid for, honest, tha knows; an' th' other's a thing as aw geet " Just then he stopped, for they'd reyelied th' station, an' th' ticket collector wet onto em in a jiffy. Tom looked a bit uneasy; but he dudn'd need. Th' collector war just the cswt as Dan hod bin thinkin' abeawt—a regular green customer, as bed never bin much to th' skoo. Tom handed him his ticket, an' Dan handed him cofe of his, but not th'reet un. Neaw this ticket as Dan gave th' collector wer a ticket for Hamilton's Excursions, them panorama fooak, yo know--an id bed sumrnat on abeawt th' " Excursions," an' underneath, i big letters,— "THROUGH EUROPIa !"

_ Th' collector stared at id a bit, an then at Dan. Dan looked o reet. Then th' collector Beret his heead, an' give him n th' card back, as innocent as a child. " Let's see,' he said to Dan, " You'll want that ticket again further on ri "Aye," said Dan, " aw couldn'd like to part wi' it yet." "Right l" said th' collector, an' off he went, quite satisfied. Dan flung his gradely ticket through th' opposite window, an' gave Torn th' bit o card to look at. When Tom read wod wer on id. he brast eawt laughin', an he'd hardly finished when they geet to th' end o' th journey °together. He said he couldn'd ha thowt as Dan hed that mich wit abeawt him." "Well, aw'm sure aw should never he gi'en him credit for it, said Roger, laughing heartily. "Nor me ayther," said Captain Lol. " lie dud weel to hey his ticket wi' him, heaw't be." "0, aye," said Bill o' mi Granny's "bed ne'er ha' tried id on beawt. Aw dornd think but wod he's honest enough, is Dan; though he is a bit ov a sponge.'"

"Aw recollect," said Dan o' mi' Dad's. " hearin tell or another sharp collector on th' line, nod far fro' here. He's a chap 'at does his duty, yo know, In his way: for he'll Inv.& look at booath ordinary tickets an' contracts, every mornin' alike. One momin' two-o-thre' young chaps fro Preston wer th' train, when th' owd stick comes beawncin' in. 'Tickets, please:, he said. Everybody poo'd their ,tickets an' contracts eiwt,except one o these young fellows, an' he wer a bit ov's swell. Th' collector looked at o th' other tickets,an' then turned to him. Your ticket, please." Contract,' answered th'. young chap, pretendin' to think thad wer enough; Nay, nay,' said th' owd un, show your ticket, sir I'm so respecter of persons.' Th' young chap poo'd a thing eawt,—an' aw'm nod sure whether id wer a season ticket for th' East Lancashire Cricket Club or nod, but heaw't be, ;A were varra like his cont act ticket, 'at wer lvin' snugly in his waistemat pocket. He handed his .club ticket up, an' th' collector med a show o' readin' th' back on 't varra keerfully. Right, right ! " he said," yo see I'm no respecter o' per- sons." An' he went smilin' eawt, quite satisfied, for he couldn't read a line on't. " Capital ! " exclaimed the old scholar, "we must look that old fellow up, and see if we can't get him pensioned off.—From The Prestan Guardian.

div.head: FASTING ITALIAN.
div.p: THE FASTING ITALIAN.

A "Star" man who saw Succi just as he com- menced the thirtieth day of his fast was, on the whole, struck with the evidence of staying powers which he still showed. Succi has now passed the limit of his longesa fast, and he naturally shows a little more nervousness than usual in beginning a new experiment. His face is drawn, as if in pain, the eyes are rather wild, and mournful, and the lines are deep about the eyes, the forehead being con- tracted into a kind of nervous frown, while there is a deep furrow in either cheek. But the hands are not thinner than those of an ordinarily thin mat, and the evidence of general emaciation is nothing startling. He responds to the salutation.of visit ors with a wave of the hand and a little smile and bow, but avoids all unnecessary muscular action. The hand in which he writes his autographs is still singularly clear, firm, and bold. He thinks he will last, and certainly there is no appearance of danger- ous weakness or any visible sign of approaching collapse.

div.head: OLD COACH ROAD TO LIVERPOOL
div.p: THE OLD COACH ROAD TO LIVERPOOL
No. 2.-Br ALFRED RIMNEIL.
The interest of this subject gathers strength from the circumstances that the mail coach service be-

tween Manchester and Liverpool was revived on a limited scale on Monday last. Resuming my account of the old road,in bygone days a short halt was made at Warrington, which is nearly equi-distant between Liverpool and Manchester, for refreshments and to change horses. The Ta bo t and the Nag's Head are the two inns mentioned in Mr. Weblis careful guide of 1822,but some custom went to the' others. Taking the figures as Mr. Webb gives them, it would seem that in the Liverpool coaches 120 horses must have been changed daily. The country which the coaches ' ran through from Warrington to Prescot is excel- ently suited for the par pose from its flatness. I•ara told by those who were in the habit of going to Liverpool in coaching days that snowstorms did not cause much inconvenience. This was a great trouble not only in hilly districts but in the eastern counties when snowstorms of great violence swept over the country from the North Sea. In one of his happiest moments Dickens describes a storm that he actually was in on his road to the Nortk. This is in "Nicholas Nickleby," in the fifth chapter :—" The night and the snow came on together, and dismal enough they were. There was no sound to be heard but the howling of the wind, for the noise of the wheels and the tread of the horses' feet were rendered inaudible by the thick coating of snow which covered the earth and was fast increasing every moment. The streets of Stamford were deserted as they passed through the town, and its old churches rose frowning and dark from the whitened ground." The upset of the coach ia the snow half way between Grantham and Newark is a record of an adventure that had re- cently happened to Dickens. The great snowstorm of 1836, which commenced in the North of England, cer- tainly impeded the mails for a few hours, but that was a trifle te what occurred in the South. Coaches were abandoned on the road, and some were stopped for a whole night, blocked up within a few miles,from London. For two days London was shut off from a great part Of England. The Manchester gown mail only reached of. Albans, where it was blooked•And afterwards upset, and the guard returned to London with the mails. A Western papersays of Manchester—" The principal roads which have been rendered for a time impassable are the roads to Sheffield by Glossop and the Woodlands, the London road in the south of Warwickshire, also between dshbourne and Derby " • but the roads to the west of Manchester were, it said, "free from any considerable obstruction." . The railway between Liverpool and Manchester, which was °petted In September, 1830, had so astonished the public with its 'access, that it was clear the days of coaching were numbered; yet in 1831 a perfect host of new coaches started from Manchester to London, princi- pally owned by John Knowles, and the Peacock, the Royal Hotel, and the Swan were for a time the scenes ef great activity. Warrington, which forms such a happy centre between the two great cities lies in the hundred of West Derby. Mr. John Ireland tila:okburne was formerly lord of the manor, but now that dignity belongs to the Corporation. According to Emerson, the first stage coach In England was started here, and here the first Lancashire newspaper was printed. Howard's work on prisons was printed here, and many other notable books came from the press of the Eyres. From Warrington the coach road passes by Hatton Hall, which has been a pleasant residence in its time, but it is now a farm house. A labourer lives at the lodge, and the bow win- dows of the drawing-room look over haystacks and a farmyard. This is by the Sankey Brook navigation, which was opened in 1755. The road has lost much even of the artificial interest that belonged to it, such as old houses and trees. It is now lined with works and work- men's cottages. About three miles from Warrington it reaches the lodges of Bold Hall. This is one of the state- ly mansions of Lancashire, and is situated in a park about two miles in length, if we take it from the War- rington road to the Burtonwood road. The hall was built in the early part of last century, and is a noble example of Italian architecture as made to do duty in England. The place is very commodious and artistic. For some time the hall has been empty, though it would seem to be a tempting residence. There is a careful oil p aint- ing left of the old Bold Hall among ths family archives, and it would seem to have been a splendid specimen of black-and=whife architecture. There was a moat round it, and Dr. Leigh gives an interesting account of the wild fowl there. The wild ducks were numerous in all South Lancashire, and bred on marshy ponds. and morasses. They especially favoured such places as Bold, where there were keepers. Rainhill, which is next reached, has some traces of picturesqueness, but its in- tiquities have vanished. Prescot, the birthplace of John Kemble, is well situated on high ground,and looks rather picturesque as we approach it, but the town has little interest. The church, which is a valuable living, is quite a wreck, and has no antiquity left. Soon after leaving Prescot we reach a succession of finely built mansions, which extend for some five miles out of Liver- pool, and are in well-kept grounds. Great interest will attach to the present movement for facilitating the dis- tribution of:parcels, which seems to have been well de- vised for the public interest.—From the Manchester Guardian.

INAUGURATION OF THE MAIL COACHES SERVICE. The parcels mail service by road between Liverpool and MancheStat was inaugurated on Monday night, ' when the first coach to be despatched from either places I started on its journey. The departure of the, coach from the Liverpool office was witnessed by a lai crowd, who cheered it heartily, as it left the post office yard. The tune allowed for the journey between Liverpool and Manchester is a little over five hours, the coach leaving at ten at night, aad being timed to arrive at its destin- ation at 3.15. a.m.,.allowing for an average rate of tra- velling of seven miles an hour. The coach on Monday night was drawn by three magnificent bays, and the turn out presented a very smart appearance, the driver (Henry Buckley) and the guard (John Thomas) being seated on the box. The first stopping place out of Liverpool is Preacot, where horses are changed. At War- rington the mail is met by a parcel post van from Wigan, and after Warrington is left horses.are again changed 1 at Hollins-green. The guards of both coaches, who are old soldiers, are suppded with horns to herald the ap- I proacb of their coaches, after the fashion of old coaching days. They are also armed with a sword bayonet and six-chambered revolver, to defend the mails in case of an attask by highway men. A large number of the prin- cipal as well as subordinate officials of Canning-place assembled to witness the despatch of the first mail, a vigorous blast being blown on the horn by Thomas as the coach was driven away. The coach from Manchester to Liverpool started punc- tually at ten o'clock from the parcel office in Stevenson- square, some thousands of people having assembled there to witness the inauguration of the service. The van was well filled with parcels, and its departure, which was announced by the blowing of a horn, was loudly cheered by the crowd of people. The vehicle was , followed down the main streets of the city by some hundreds of spectators. In connection with the new ; service a single horse mail coach is run between South- port and Liverpool and vice versa, calling at Formby, Blundellsands, Waterloo, Seaforth, and Bootle.

CHECK M ATED. TUE first object upon which Martin's °yea alighted was the figure of Mr. Dick Worrell, got up in the latest style of sporting costume, and seated astride of a high stool, as if it were a saddle, while he refreshed himself with hot sausage, one of a score seething and bubbling in a tin dish over a gas jet, potatoes. and a mug of bitter beer. Ah, Marty," he said, with his mouth full, "come and try a eorsidge; they're just prime. Sorsidge, titters, an' mug bitter, my dear," he said to the attendant. There were quite a dozen psople eating and drinking in the narrow bar, so that Martin felt that it was no time for &berg of rage. Ile could not, however, refrain from grasping Dick Worrell by the arm, and whisper- ing, sharply: "You scoundrell How dare you send to me at the office?" "Gently, old 'un." said Dick. "Don't shove a fellow's knife down his throat. Here, hold hard a minute; here's your sorsidge. You may as well pay for both of these pecks." Martin writhed, but he was in the toils; and, as the attendant waited, he took out a florin and laid it upon the counter. "Now, then," whispered Martin, "perhaps you'll answer my question." "Certainly, dear boy. What is it?" "I say," repi;ed Martin, striving hard to be cool, "why did you drag me from the office after what I had said?" " Here's to you," said the fellow, with provoking coolness, as he raised the electro-plated mug and began to drink slowly, raising the vessel higher tied higher till he could look through the cleat glass bottom at Martin's wrathful face. "Why did I send tor you, old man? "said Worrell, with provoking coolness. "Yes. Why did you not wait till to-night, instead of sending that meesage ? " " Oh," was the laughing reply, "it was because I wanted the money now. Lookye here, dear boy," con- tinued Worrell," it's no good for you to look fierce, and to kick like that. Bat your snack like a man, and drink your bitter, and just listen to what I've got to say." "1 can't stop now; I must go back.' "But you must stop," said WorralL "You've got to stop. I want you." He fixed his eyes upon those of Martin, and for a few moments they remained like that without blinking, Martin quite livid, and Worrell keeping up an ugly smile, whites disfigured his unpleasant countenance. " You seem to forget two or three little things, dear boy," continued Worrell; "and its very unpleasant for me to have to tell yeu about them; but when I do tell you, Imean it to he nicely in company, don't you see, BO Be to keep you from going into one of your ugly tempera, and running risks. You see you're such a passionate sort o' 'hap, and might be getting yourself into trouble for trying to do me a mischief—ebucking me into the river, or some other game of that kind that you'd be sorry for after, because it's no use for you to say you don't like me; I know you do." There was that set of grinning, great white teeth hared before Martin again, and his fingers involuntarily clinched together, as if he were about to strike a blow; but he knew that he dared not, and again he had to force down his rage. "Au. that's better," said Worrell, bending towards him. "Now you look seraible ones more. Look here, Martin, old lad." He laid his learns, thick-nailed hand upon the young man's shoulder familiarly, and whispered a few words in his ear. Martin shuddered as much at the contact of the fellow's hand as at the words he uttered. "What do yen say to it, eh? Wouldn't it be prime? Good haul, and no risk. Set ton clear. make a man of you. Why, Marty, you'd be so flush o' money, you'd be able to cut all your acquaintances. 'specially me." He was already very dose to Martin, but at this point he premed nearer, and bared his great white teeth more and more. "Now, then, what do you say?" whispered Worrell, watching the young man intently, while the business of the place went on. "No, no; it's impossible I— eh?" He started violently, and turned with a guilty look in his fat*, just as a man might who had been antici- pating arrest, and the officer's touch upon his shoulder had come at last. There, with a peculiar smile upon his countenance, stood Samson Hall, who sodded at him familiarly, gave his head a side nod towards 'Worrell, and then left the place. "Why, that's your messenger chap, isn't it?" said Worrell. "Yes," cried Martin, wrathfully; "and he'll tell them at the office that he saw us together." "Very well," said. Worrell, arranging his tie and the gaudy pin that was stuck ostentatiously therein. He can only say he saw you talking to a gentleman at a refreshment bar, and having a snack. There aint no harm in that, I should hope." In the bitterness of his spirit Martin could have laughed aloud at his companion's conceit; but there was tou much at stake, and he turned as if to go. "Where are you going ? • said WorralL "Back to the office." "-Not till we've settled that bite' business, dear boy, and the other little bet as welL" see you - to-night at the old place,' cried Martin. "Must go now." "All right: at the old place, at the usual time, of course and Worrell descended from his stool. "Where are you going now?" said Martin, in slam. "Back along with you now. It's all right, I know, my boy. Old Copperstick is ill, and there's only out dear brother there, and he'll bleed like a lamb." " Do you mean that you will come straight to the office with me?" "flight away, as they say on the underground. Come along; but ain't you going to finish your bitter?" Martin "Moolford stood gazing straight before bra, checkmated by her companion's. familiar tacties ; and, in the perspective that opened out before him, he ones more saw how by his folly he had allowed himself to be made the tool of the scoundrel by his side. It was of no use, he told ';rneelf, to fight, and drawing a long breath through his clenched teeth, he gave in. Well ? " said Worrell, sharply. "Yes: I agree." "That's right; but I knew you would. And now about that other trifling matter: I welt that money." "I haven't got it." "Then you must get it," was the uncompromising rejoinder. " Yes," said Martin, "I suppose I must. ru bring it to the old place to-night." "What time?" "Not till late: say twelve." "That'll do," said Worrell; "only I shall wait till you do bring it. Leastwise, I shall wait till I'm obliged to go; and if tour very late, old man, don't trouble, for I'll call in at your °filet; for it in the morning, and have a chat with that messenger chap of yours till you come." "I shall be sure and come," said Martin, hoarsely; and he left the place, while hopping, clumsily on to the stool once more, DickWorrall indulged in a hearty internal laugh. "For,' be said to himself, "how easy I can manna that chap. Why, if I could get bold of a couple more like him, and put 'em as tightly under my thumb, I could 'tend every race all round, aad live like a prince,"

MARK WOOLFORD oiten sat and tried to solve the difficult question before him, and wondered whether he was doing right. His heart told him that Ruth's induence was not working as he wished, and as be had fully expected ; and if he Enid she could rot lead his brother back to a better life than that wtich he feared he was leading, to what a fate was tie poor girl condemning herself, while he stood by vithout stretching forth a hindering hand. What ought he to do? he asked himser—step between them and stay all futuro intercourse, or let matters take their course? These were questions which he could not ansver ; for how could he step in between, and act as judge when his partial heart was ready to go against one of the parties in the suit? Be ended, as he had often ended before, by ciaciding to let things drift, in the hope that some cours, might suggest itself by which he would be able tc escape from what was rapidly assuming the fore of a terrible dilemma; and this at a time when Rut] often sought her own room, where she sat and gobbet ready to break her heart. her great troubles being lartin's careless ways, and the reckless course he puwued— troubles these that at times seemed almost greaer than she could bear. On the evening of the day when Martin lad en- countered Dick Worrell, Mark returmd, acceding to custom, to the late dinner in Brunswick-spar. "Martin come back?" he said. cheerfully.

-110; 851 a Min iciopetocz, witn a ea.sse bead, and a vicious rub at one of her ears--a real sign that she was vexed., ii Mark turned to Ruth, and was about to ask her she knew whether his brother woald be back to dinner; but she seemed to divine what he was about to Kilo and shrank from him with so scared an aspect that the words died away upon his lips. "It would only give her pain, poor child," be thought; and he passed the matter off with some sommon-place remark, taking his seat directly after- wards ; and, in spite of his attempts to he oheerful, uS seemed to have brought a chill with him into the house. Miss Klopstock proved to be the most conversational of the trio, but her remarks did not conduce to hilarity; and Martin's empty place was constantly drawing attention to his absences Miss Klopstock was the worthiest of elderly laiies; but, like most ladies of a certain age, she bad ' peculiarities of her own, foremost among which wee thorough belief in portents. If two knives happened to be crossed upon it meant one thing; if a kettle was upset, it meant another. Three sneezes indicated a very serious mishap, and the yawn of a cat something decidedly worse. You could not make her believe that throwing table, three pinches over the left shoulder would not avert the coming mischief if you upset the salt; while the appearance of floating twigs suggestive of birch broom neup of tea—those scraps generally knewn ee strangers "—had a peculiar signifloation in her eyes, which she never ventured to interpret to unbelieving souls. For some time past it bad been the custom at the Woolford's to speak of Miss Klopstock as "Au' It was a convenient term, and it had been accepted by the old lady years before in the most serious way. Ruth being the only one who could, when so eddress- ing her, draw from her a smile. On this particular evening, " Aunt" was extremell fidgetty. The gravy spoon had tw;ce shooed into the dish while Mark was carving, and had to be taken out of the room and wiped. "Ruth, my dear, said the old lady; "if that sPoell. slips into the gravy again, I shall not like it." "Neither shall I," said Mark, trying to be cheerful; and as he spoke he smiled at Ruth, whose troubled looks gave him pain. "Yes, you may sneer, Mark," exclaimed the old lady; "but it is not a matter to be treated with levity. I saw you smile across the table at Ruth, and it :s not at all becoming." "My dear aunt," he exclaimed, "I was only swill' at the possibility of baying a greasy tables Pea to hold, and—tut I tut! tut! There it noes again. "Just as I expected," exclaimed Miss Klopstock• That makes three times the spooo hiss glided into the dish." "Right under the loin of mutton," said Dlst,

quietly. "And amongst the gravy," said Miss Klopstockt , " Whiels is now growing cold, and becoming coato° with imitation :sixpences," continued Mark, smiling once more across the table at Ruth, who this 0'55 ' responded, and was caught in the act by Miss Klor stock. d • "Laugh as much as you please, Mark Woolfor, she said, purting down her knife and fork, and sbaldog her head at him; "but don't try and inoculate thin poor child with your scepticism. Mark, you neve° believe in anything." "Yes, I do," replied Mark. "I believe to° • thoroughly in you." "Maybe, she said, refusing to be softened by thw adroit compliment, for which Mark was rewarded Ij' Ruth with a look which made his heart beat faster, Reason stepped in, and told him it was folly. "Come," he said, merrily. "Now what is it a - of when the gravy spoon slips into the dish?', 'Pr "Don's you mock and jibe, Mark Woolford," ol"r7t Miss Klopstoek ; "and dent smile like that, becao° does not become you. Yours is not a pleasant cast ° counts/Fleece for a laugh." "Perhaps she is right," said Mark to himself. come," be cried aloud, "you do not tell us." to "It's a sign of something very unoleasant abont id happen," said Miss Klopstock. oracularly, as sh°l2-e'4 np one finger. "I do not say what it is, nor who° ' will be; buttvhen we have three warnings within coo hour, somettring very serious must be coming t° pan. "May I ask what other warniag we have had: osia Mark. Miss Klopstook snorted and tossed her head, Nell too angry to epeak ; but she w•as too muoix suited 5° ' bent upon her theme to keep anything back. she "My left forefinger has tiagled this evening, . maid severely; "and three times over that cat has ' up on her hind legs to claw at the chair-cover. I. hardly needed that slipping of the gravy spoon to °I vince me of coining trouble." Mark glanced at Ruth, and saw, or fancied t176,,,t be„, eaw, traces in her face of a faint belief in Miss to°Y stisek's opinions, so he said: 'Don't you think something might happen svithl , our having any of these trifling domestic incidento watching cats, tingling fingers, and slipping 81:000,10 "Oh yes, of course! It is quite possible, said Klopetock, with asperity; "but it is useless to attBlo. to argue with you about such things, Mark, so we "That we will not," he said, pleasantly; " oda' not quarrel." ill dear aunt, you shall enjoy your opinions and -I enjoy mine." "Yes, but mark my words," said Min Slope.; jko evil will come, you may depend upon that, 00 notice of what I have said, "We will," said Mark; "and you are quite r]el4,o evil will come, as it does, to every home, but gO7 come, too, so we will take both patiently in turn. „of "Yes,' said Miss Klopstock, "but I never so ' a presentiment without its being feisilea, on- A will see that this will be in turn." otb4 Mark turned off the conversation into on ctbs channel, and tried hard during the latter part dinner to be cheerful, and to make hi° (I°ort pardons the same, but, try bow he would, seemed to be a chill resting upon all: one kept glancing at the vacant cheir, of thinking of the absentee; and, in sPite„,solg, his efforts and a tolerably strong mind, for the life of him, could not help recalling, .4,,g Klepstook's oracular utterances, and nono7o-30i whether people ever did receive warnings or terrible misfortune before it came.

A steldv increase of prosperity had, he exe,,u,„l.lse,ll the estimates which prudence dictated to in the result by £3,000,000 sterling, while th,ll—ated expenditure had not been exceeded by —4 £llB,OOOl During last year the country
4**ttff

seemed to have come upon a real period of prosperity' and the result had been that in some respects the estimates showed a very remarkable elasticity, nearly £2,00),000 out of the surplus of £3,250,000 in revenue over estimate being due to an extraordinary rush to alcohol. The duty on companies' capital had yielded £290,000, against an estimate of £lBO,OOO. Dur- ing the past three years the National Debt had been re- duced by £23,323,000, the largest amount ever reduced in any three censecutive years of the national history. After mentioning that he intended in a few, days to introduce a bill dealing with light gold, Mr. Goschen submitted his proposals for the ensuing year. It was proposed to set aside £lOO,OOO for the equipment of Volunteers, and to reduce the rate of postage to India and the Colonies to 24d. With regard to the income, tax, it was proposed to allow a man who had a profit under one schedule and a loss under another to set off the one against the other. It was proposed to remit the duty on gold and silver, and to reduce the duty on tea 2d. per lb., and on currants by ss. per ewt., also to reduce the inhabited house duty en all houses rented under £6O a year. It was proposed to put for local purposes a surtax of 6d. per gallon on British and foreign spirits, the increased duty of 3d. placed on beer last year to be takenoff in the Imperial Budget, but reimposed year local purposes. The Government intended to propose ci suspensory measure whereby there should be no further issue of licenses until the whole question was settled, unless under exceptional circumstances. A formal resolution with regard to the duty on spirits having been read, Sir W. Harcourt, regretting the unavoidable absence of Mr. Gladstone paid Mr. Goschen a graceful compliment on hisstatemene, butsaid it showed that Free Trade had not caused the commercial depression ad that bimetallism was not needed to restore the finances of the country. He wished Mr. Goschen had remitted the duty on houses under £lOO a year, and asked, seeing that he had two millions at his disposal, what ho intended to do in the matter of assisted educa- tion, to which the Government had pledged themselves. Mr. Howard Vincent, Mr. Rathbone, Mr. Broadhurst, Mr. Mundella, and other members took part in the debate, some expressing regret that Mr. Goschen had not seen his way' to take a penny off the income tax. Mr. Goschen replied, the formal Budget resolutions were agreed to, and the House adjourned at thirty-five minutes past twelve o'clock.

STRIKE OF MANCHESTER TAILORS.

The strike of Jewish tailors in Manchester continues. On Tuesday the men, to the number of about 1,200, paraded the streets from Cheetham to Albert Square, and walked thence to Stevenson Square, where they held a meeting. Speeches were made by the leaders of the movement. The position of the Jewish workers was described as little better than slavery, and Mr. Kelley, secretary of the Manchester and Salford Trades Council, said they had the fullest sympathy and support of that body. In the afternoon an excited meeting, attended by both masters and strike hands, was held in the Assembly- roont of the Free Trade Hall. A conference of representa- tives of both sides was recommended, but the meeting arrived at no definite decision. . .

On Wednesday demands for a rise in wages on behalf of the English Working Tailors' Union in Manchester were made public, and it is feared that unless moderate counsels prevail another strike will result.

div.head: TIPPERARY DEMONSTRATION.
div.p: THE TIPPERARY DEMONSTRATION.

The inauguration of New Tipperary on Saturday was attended by several English Liberal members, including Mr. J. A. Picton, M.P.' Mr. R. Leake, M.P., Mr. C. E. Schwann' M.P., and Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. Lady Sandhurst was present as representing the Liberal women of England. There was a large gathering of Irish repre- sentatives. Addresses to the English visitors were pre- sented on behalt of the Tipperary Town Commissioners and of the Tenants' Defence Committee.—Replying for the English members of Parliament, Mr. Picton said that on the personal question he would offer- no opinion. What he and his colleagues rejoiced in was the fact that of the two combinations—the landlords and the tenants— that of the tenants had proved itself the stronger. He was greatly impressed with the evidences of self-sacrifice which he saw around him.—Lady Sandhurst also spoke, and the gathering was afterwards addressed by the Lord Mayor of Dublin and by Mr. Davitt.—Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., then discharged the task of declaring the mart of New Tipperary open for traffic, and in doing so he delivered an eloquent address. In the evening there was a banquet, presided over by Canon Cahill.—Mr. Schwann proposed the toast of "New Tipperary."— Mr. W. O'Brien, who was enthusiastically cheered on rising to reply, spoke of the glorious stand the men of Tipperary had made against one of the most formidable landlord conspiracies, against one of the most brutal systems of police tyranny that had ever been directed 'against the homes and liberties of the Irish people.—Mr. I R. Leaks, M.P., proposed" Ireland a Nation," and Mr. 'Michael Devitt replied. Other toasts followed, including " Our English Visitors," proposed by Mr. J. O'Connor, I M.P., and acknowledged by Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., I and others.

div.head: _ CHESHIRE STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE.
div.p: _ CHESHIRE STANDING JOINT COM- MITTEE.

The quarterly meeting of this committee was held on Saturday, at Chester Castle, under the presidency of Colonel C. H. France-Hayhurst, Mr. ,Duncan Graham and Mr. James Tomkinson (chairman and vice-chairman of the county council), and his Honour Judge Horatio Lloyd (chairman of the quarter sessions), being amongst those present. On the recommendation of Colonel Hamersley, chief constable, an increase of the county constabulary by four sergeants and 24 constables, at an additioxal annual cost to the polies rate of £907, was sanctioned. The additional men are distributed as follows :—Runcorn, two constables; Macclesfield, two ; Hyde, one sergeaat and four constables; Northwich, two sergeants and three constables; Nantwich, one sergeant and five constables - Altrincham, four con- stables. The proportion of po'lice to population now is one to 1,218.

div.head: TICE NEW CLERK OF THE PEACE.
div.p: TICE NEW CLERK OF THE PEACE.

Mr. Reginald Potts, son--of the late clerk, was unanimously appointed clerk of the peace and clerk of the County Council, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Judge Lloyd. and supported by Mr. Duncan Graham, Mr. P. Speakman, Mr. Ralph Bates, and Dr. Hodgson.—On the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr. Joseph Beckett, it was resolved "That the salary of the clerk of the peace and clerk of the County Council and county solicitor, as from the Ist April, 1889, be the sum of £l,BOO per annum, and that he be allowed in addition, as from such date, the annual sum of £7OO, to cover all the expenses of his offices and duties (except parliamentary business, suits and actions, and extra clerks' hire in connectiop with the registration, sessions order books, postage of letters, carriage of parcels, print- ing, stamps, counsels' fees, agents' charges, travelling expenses, being money out of pocket), and that he be not required to devote the whole of his time to the service of the county. (The salary of the late clerk was £1,600 without the allowance of £7OO.

div.head: INCREABB OF DRVNIEENNESS.
div.p: INCREABB OF DRVNIEENNESS.

------ - Colonel Hamersley reported that there were 2,732 ap- prehended and summoned during the quarter, an in- crease of 473, attributable to the muzzling order. Ap- prehensions for vagrancy had decreased, but as to drunk- enness the report stated—" During the quarter 661 males and 109 females were proceeded against for drunkenness, and 630 males and 124 females in the game period of last year, or an increase of 31 males and a de- crease of 15 females; and in comparison with the cor- responding quarter of 1885 an increase of 169 males and 38 females. '—Replying to Mr. James Tomkinson, the Chief Constable said the increase of last quarter was not due (as on previous occasions) to the number of loafers attracted to the county by the Ship Canal Works. Mr. M. T. Graveson, of Liscard, strongly urged that more attention should be paid by magistrates to the question a where men got drunk, and expressed the opinion that if the police looked more closely after those who supplied the drink the state of things might be much Improved. THE ALLEGATIONS AGAINST THE POLICE. A letter was submitted from Mr. J. Slater Lewis, county councillor for the Frodsham Division, enclosing oorrespondence between himself and the Rome Office (already published in our columns), in which- it was alleged that members of the county constabulary were employed by landlords for the protection of game, and that a fund was in existence for rewarding policemen who secured convictions for offences against the game laws. The Home Secretary, in his reply, stated that some of Mr. Lewis's information was inaccurate, and as to the rest, he referred him to the Standing Joint Committee. Mr. C. Lister, a member of the Committee and a county magistrate, also read some correspondence be- tween Mr. Lewis and himself on this subject, in which Mr Lewis offered to lay his information before a com- mittee of five (named by himself, four being county magistrates) on condition that no one else should be pre- sent, find that each one of the committee should pledge hims 4 to secrecy beforehand. After considerable dis- cussion, the meeting, while refusing to sanctio4 the con- dition as to the pledge of secrecy, appointed tile follow- ing committee of investigation C. Lister, Mr. Duncan Graham, Mr. James Tomkiuson, Mr. Joseph Beckett, and Judge Lloyd. These were all suggested by Mr. Ltwis, with the exception of Judge Lloyd, who was substituted by the meeting for Mr. Booby, the latter not being t member of the Standing Joint Committee. A resolution providing for the holding of coroners' inquests in buitlings other than gublic-honses was carried, and the meting terminated.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 19, 1890.

has pervaded his remarks, with the exception of the un- fortunate word, which I don't think he meant, of "clique," but lam sure he speaks conscientiously, and I respect that ccuiscientious feeling. I am sure he has no feeling of want of respect to me personally. At the same time, lam sorry he used the word clique, because in the vestry we were most unanimous, and I am sure we shall all find that with our larger number of sidesmep—and I shall con- suit them in everything—there will be no clique, and we shall act, I hope, as one body. (Applause.) I won't go into the points Dr. Cannell has mentioned, though I am quite prepared to defend myself at the proper time. (Applause.) What I sincerely grieve over, and what I am sure Dr. Cannell grieves over in his heart, is that it should go forth, as it did through the papers all over the diocese, and all over the country, that we were ap- parently a parish at war and that a bad feeling existed among us. Don't believe that for a moment. I can point to various signs, not with pride, but with the greatest thankfulness. I see our church full. (Hear, hear.) I see our offertory large—£2o more than last year—and last tear was considerably in excess of the year before. We had over 300 communicants on Easter Day ; there was a large number of candidates for confir- mation, we had a large number the year before. I may say one thing more; that the amount of the offertory represents by no means the large sums given for all kinds of purposes in the parish, and in a few days you will have a statement, issued in a form which you can under- stand, showing what has been collected and what has been spent in the parish during the past twelve months. All these are signs under God of success. We have a large body of workers. I don't for a moment expect everyone to think as I do. It is only reasonable to expect changes when a new man comes into an old parish—the late Rector being an old man—though at his age I shan't do half he did. Work was left undone which I had to do. There came in some changes. I don't expect all to agree with me in everything. and more men know me they will see that. I don't in the lost wish or care to carry out my own views. All I care for is to preach the faith delivered to the saints as I understand it. believe I shall bring men to see with me in time. All don't now, but I am sure they will learn to respect and love me. The meeting then broke up.

div.head: PARISH CIIIJROII VESTRY MEETING.
div.p: PARISH CIIIJROII VESTRY MEETING.
DR. CANNELL DETAILS MS OBJECTIONS.

An adjourned meeting in vestry of the parishioners of St. Elphins' was held in the National School-room, Church-st., cn Saturday evening, the Rector, the Rev. F. W. Willis, in the chair. The meeting had been ad- journed in consequence of the unusual circumstance of a poll having been demanded in regard to the election of the people's warden. Mr. Alfred Woods and Dr. Cannell were nominated, and the former received a large majority of votes,whereupon Dr. Cannelldemanded a poll, with the object of testing the feeling of the pariihioners with re- gard to alleged ritualistic practices by the rector, the Rev. F. W. Willis. Subsequently objection was taken to the voting qualification of Dr. Carmen's seconder, and as the vestry-clerk upheld the objection and advised the rector to declare Mr. Woods elected, the poll fell through. The matter was freely discussed in the town ,and when the adjourned meeting was held on Saturday night there was a very large assembly of parishoners, a scene being anticipated.

div.head: ELECTION OF PEOPLE'S WARDEN.
div.p: THE ELECTION OF PEOPLE'S WARDEN.

At the commencement of the proceedings the Rector said that they would have gathered from the papers that Dr. Cannell's candidature had fallen through. He was sure they would all be glad that they had been spared the cost, and the anxiety, and the probable bad feeling, that a poll would have caused. It remained for him now to declare Mr. Alfred Woods duly elected. (Applause.)
