DR. CARRELL AND "THE PRACTICES AT THE CHURCH." At the close of the ordinary business of the meeting, Dr. Cannel' said :—I should like it to be distinctly under- stood in the first place that I do not come to the vestry meeting with any hostile feeling. I come here as a matter of principle. The Rector is not the man I conse to abuse ; it is simply because of the practices of the church. There has been considerable discussion outside, and I am sorry to think that a clique of the vestry have been at the head of it.—Mr. Alfred Woods: I object to any language of this sort being used, and I think the majority of the parishioners in the room will back me out. (Applause.) As Dr. Cannell said, he is not a plough boy. I hope he does not think that we are. And if we are plough boys, there are plough boys with intellect and intelligence as well as other people. lam willing to sit here all night and listen to Dr. Cannell if he will speak correctly, and do as he would be done by to the whole of us.—Dr. Cannell: I always do, and always intend to do as I would be done by; but as Mr. Woods has made such an , assertion, I may say that within ten minutes after the vestry meeting was over I was told that there was a flaw in my nomination. I ask you, sir, if you knew my nomination was wrong. If you did I am certain you would have told me.—The Rector: Certainly.—Dr. Cannell: The Rector would have told me.—Mr. Alfred Woods : Excuse me, I did not know. I didn't know for two hours afterwards.— Dr. Cannell.—Consistency I do like, but inconsistency I dislike. Here is Mr. Woods, who has begun to talk about what he can do, and what he has done ; but I maintain that Mr. Woods knew the very morning we left the vestry, and I can mention the name of a gentlemen not one hundred million yards from his right hand who knew as much as he did. lam perfectly satisfied. lam not going to Show any spleen, or splenetic feeling. lam perfectly satisfied if I am disqualified; but I may tell you, and the public through the press, what I really object to as a parishioner. I do not wish to give offence, but, as I tell you, you teach, and I have no doubt you should teach still, 'Train up a child in tbe way it should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it." I have been trained in one sphere; that sphere I love. I cannot for the life of me see why I should take obligations belonging to other churches now. Of course yon know that in the first place I take exception to the cross. You know that adoration is not a part of the 39 Articles. I take exception to the removal of the reading desk, and the reason that desk was removed was because each time the clergyman had to pass from the prayer desk to the reading desk he had to pass the cross and adore it. I object to the innovation in the service before the sermon. I say that there is no man in the world, or on the face of the earth, who can look me in the face and tell me that he is a sacrificing pricist. We want to wor- ship no man. I worship Him above, and I say that you (the Rector), with the greatest respect for your position, which is a very honourable one, are simply a profession- al man the same as I am. You can commit sins equally with me, but still we ought to take notice of you by say- ing "Does I say, not as I do." I object to these things being brought forward. There is another matter. I cannot see why we should decorate our church with flowers. You know what the youthful mind is. If you I had studied human nature as I have done—(loud laughter, and a Voice: "Question ")—you would know perfectly well that the youthful mind is very soon dis- tracted if you place anything on the wall in the shape of a picture. You yourself may be devout in prayer, but I maintain that ornament distracts the mind. There is not the shadow of a doubt that we are as good in this room at the present time as if we had met in any parish church in England. I hope, Rector, I have given no offence in the stand I have made, and when the next Easter vestry meeting comes round I shall be prepared either to find a candidate or contest the matter to see what the parish + says. 'lf the parish is found to •be decidedly against me I shall be perfectly satisfied ; I will nurse my own grievance, but I wish it to go forth th the publie that I have not come here to give you (the Rector), or any other parishioner any offence. The Mayor : Dr. Cannell made use of the word " clique " in the vestry. When I went out of that vestry I fully believed we should have had a poll here to-day.—Dr. Cannell: You did, Mr. Mayor.—Mr. Alfred Woods: And so did I, Dr. Cannell.—The Mayor: I never thought Mr. Beacon was disqualified in consequence of living out of the parish. / feel certain that the Rector and most of those who attended the vestry meeting thought the same. lam sure that none of us want to see anything unfair done.

div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE AT HULL.
div.p: ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE AT HULL.

A terrible tragedy occurred at Hull early on Tuesday morning. A fisherman, named George Broadley, ac- companied a woman named Eliza Reynolds, to her home in Gordon-avenue, Woodcock-street, Hull, on Monday night, and insisted on staying the night. She refused. and ordered him to leave the house. Broadley produced a loaded revolver, and the terrified woman made ready to go back to the room with him. Watching her oppor- tunity, she, in a semi-nude state, ran out of the house, but was fetched back by Broadley. She was more successful afterwards, and, reaching Gordon-st. Police Station, gave the alarm. Broadley, while pursuing her, was intercepted by Police Constable Wright. Seeing capture inevitable, Broadley fired twice at the policeman, just missing his head, and then placing the revolver against his own head, fired and killed himself.

div.head: EASTER VESTRY BATTLE.
div.p: THE EASTER VESTRY BATTLE.
BY KO-110.
" The flowers that bloom in the spring, tra-la,

Rave nothing to do with the ease.' That may be true in some cases, ladies and gentle- men, but it is not so in the case of Mr. Robert Foulkes, of Frodsham. The bearing of the quota- tion lies in its application, flowers, he thinks, when ever they bloom, are all right in their way, but when you stick 'era up in church, tra-la, they have a good deal to do with the case. And the case of Mr. Robert Foulkes is a bard one, or Mr. Robert Foulkes is a hard case, which ever way you like to take it. _ _

I make no apology to the gentleman for introduc- ing him to you in this summary fashion. He likes to see himself in print, and is much given to writ- ling very perplexing headachy letters, principally composed of texts end quotation marks, to the Editor of this paper—not so much "as a guarantee of good faith,' as publintion." Why the Editor prints them is a mystery known only to himself. Perhaps, like me, he does .not understand them; and perhaps, unlike me, he does not care to say so. However, that is a matter between- him and his clients. For my part, I think some explanation is idue for mentioning Mr. Foulkee at all. I do not want to hurt his sensitive feelings. The flowers in the church do that, and trouble him grievously. I simply want to use him as a peg on which to hang my discourse—to trot him round the ring as a preliminary canter to the show to follow. Just now levity is far remqved from my thoughts, though most visuredly Phad much rather be dealing with a less serious subject than the one on hand. To poke fun at Mr. Foulkes, who is the very embodiment of the man with a grievance, is not to poke fun at the cause he champions.i which s the sacred cause of religion—as he views it. Neither would I poke fun at the persons present at the recent vestry meeting at Frodsham at which Mr. Foulkes was the odd man out, as they champion the same sacred cause—from their point of view. What I am suffering from, as well as a great many others, is the after-effects of the great Easter religious squabble, in which certain disaf- fected parties like Mr. Foulkes have, according to , their lights—which lights they never by any, chance hide under a bushel—taken a very prominent part. At this season of the year the Church of England seem‘to be turned into a battlefield, on which the Saints tilt at each other with their fads and opinions,l and say nasty things at each other, much to the dis- gust of many upright Sinners and greatly to the de- light of those who sit in the Seat of the Scornful. "A Stormy Vestry Meeting," "An Indignant Par- ishioner." 'A Vicar Censured," and the -like, have been common enough headings in all the newspapers lately, and they have generally got big type and a good position amongst the news of the day as well. The sapient sub-editors of a portion of the Press no doubt think the public dote on such matters. That must be " taking ' reading that details the strug- gling of a few Christians about a few flowers, or about a cross! It really, of necessity, must. But the fact is, that a great proportion of sensible readers don't care a jot about such things. If it is to be, they think, that parishioners must bark and bite at each other, and their vicars, let them d• it quietly, and let peaceable men remain with their peace undisturbed by such bickering.. These who do not read these things, take no harm. But how, about those who do read them? Are they notl likely to think that the Church is being brought I into disrepute? These remarks, of course, apply particularly to the Church as an establishment, and not to the Dissenting portion of the commu- nity, who seem to knock along pretty harmoniously. The fact of the matter is that a portion of the Churchmen of this country have got it into their heads that the Church is rapidly going to the dogs —which in this case means Rome. Mr. Foulkes thinks so, and so seem to think some of the parish- ioners of St. Elphin's. in this good old town. There- fore, they are like unto dogs with sore ears—always on the scratch. But is their allegation true? I think not. It seems to be the idea that a number of the clergymen of the Church of England are gradually introducing the thin edge of the wedge, and that before we know it we shall all find our- selves under the dominion of his Holiness the Pope. Ritualism is the rock on which we are to come to grief. It may be a fact that in some churches cer- tain innovations are being made in the direction of what is called Ritualism, but England is essentially a Protestant country, and if there was such a thing as a general attempt on the part of those in autho- rity to slip over to Rome, it wouldn't come off. Not in the least; the only result would be the disestab- lishment of the church, and, between you and I, it might be best if that happened, for there would then be an end of many a "Church Dispute." But I deny that there is any such attempt, either general or local. As a rule the objections that are made so much Of, all upon principle mind, are too trivial to be noticed. Take the case of Frodsham. Mr. Foulkes said— " They could not find in St. Paul's Instructions to the Churches that they had to have flowers inside. In that church they had a cross which was not legal, and to get out of it they had to put up a little rear table. He moved that the ladies keep their flowers at home, as they were not required for the purposes of worship, and tended to distract the mind." Phew! What a pity for the mind to be so distracted. This is his first objection, on prin- ciple, of course; and what a weak, little, shrivelled up thing it is. An insult to the flowers, too. How did the meeting take it? "Mr. Foulkes did hot find a seconder," but he was not crushed. The "Runcorn Examiner "of last week says he was excited. I wasn't there, but judging from the report, he must have been. He next proposed the substitution of another hymn book in the place of Hymns Ancient and Modern, which, he said, contained 100 Popish hymns. He furthermore made use of some very strong remarks, but as, a second time, he received no support to his proposition, the Vicar moved that the vestry proceed with the next business. This the obstructionist described as" a Jesuitical trick," and thereby showed his hand. He was like one crying in the wilderness, for all the effect his out- pourings had. And because he was right, and all

the others were wrong, there must, of course, he a " Jesuitical trick " lurking in some corner or ot her. Judging from this, as one case, however, it would really seem as though Mr Foulkes was wrong, and the rest of the meeting right ; that is, if we are to stick to the idea that majorities rule. The moral of which is that Mr. Foulkes had better join some other church, or build a brand-new one for himself —the latter suggestion preferred. Had he had any- thing in the way of a following, the matter would have been different. The Vicar of Frodsham, like all other Vicars, can pretty well please himself what course he takes in these little matters, but it it had been that any considerable portion of his parishioners seemed to wish things different, he would no doubt have tried to meet their views. But when it is a question of pleasing Mr. Foulkes at the expense of the rest, he very wisely declines to do it, and Mr. Foulkes really ought to take a back seat. Then there is the case of Dr. Cannell and the Warrington vestry, which, as it seems to me, is one of another type altogether. He was a great deal more temperate in his manner of formulating objections, and does not go about continually screeching a crusade against Ritualism. Again, he does seem to iiave partners in distress, and honestly believes that he would have a majority of the parish with him. I doubt that myself, but if it should be the case it would only be a graceful and a proper act on the part of the Rector to meet the objections with every consideration. Dr. Cannel' has made his protest, the matter is passed, and it is to be hoped that it will not rise again. In this case also the majority will rule, for I don't think the Rector is pigheaded, or the man to scout the wishes of the majority of his flock. But apart from the right or wrong of these particular cases, I isn't it a pity to see so much dissension in the ranks of religion 7 Isn't it a pity that men must not only have a lot of different ways to get to [leaven, but that they must needs quarrel as to whose way is the best? You had a letter in your paper on Saturday, the writer of which seemed filled in component pasta with two desires—one to show the wickedness of Roman Catholicism and the other to make it known that he has been to France. This week you may have another on the other side of the question. It would puzzle one to say how many sects there are at the present time—even how many sects there are marching in different directions towards the Golden Gates under the banner of Protestantism. And each sect thinks it alone is right. All the rest are on the broad path that leads to somewhere else. Think how many Roman Catholics there must be in the world, how many Protestants, how many Moham- medans, and who dare say that any one of these religions, as religions, have not an equal chance of Heaven. If you must go there by different routes, go in peace, and let others go in peace also. Let it ito longer be said in scorn—" How these Christians love one another!" Take unto yourselves more christian charity. In my salad days, I lived in a country where there are many Mahommedana, and among them cleanliness of living, strictness of morals, devout- ness, and well-doing, were by no means uncom- mon. Who shall say that their future shall not be as blissful as that of the most righteous amonz you? Some, no doubt, would think not, but how absurd. To what extremes can fanaticism go! Will the day ever come when there will be one Universal Church on earth? There does not seera much chance of it. The missionaries of our various churches are penetrating to the uttermost parts of the world, each disposing of his particular religious wares. and thus the schisms are widened. What will the untutored savage think of it all, with one lot pull- ing him one way, and another the other. Some who have had a glimpse of missionary work among the untutored ones, seem to think they generally take the way that will pay best in a worldly sense. Civilisation, when there is not too much rum about it, may be on the whole a good thing for the heathen, but if the various churches are all trying to induce them to go spiritually in different directions, it may go rather hard with the churches. The moral of which is that philanthropic persons might very well direct a little more of their money and philanthropy to the heathen at home, and give those abroad a rest. In any case, to con- clude, if it must be that there shall be all these splits in the religous world, for goodness sake let us have more peace about it, less bittevness, more good-will and christian charity. Else can we be surprised if the thoughtful man eschews our Taber- nacles, and takes himself on Sundays to the fields and country lanes, to the babbling brooks and the company of the trifling birds, to look from Nature up to Nature's God, and, perhaps, in so doing, to find himself at peace. _

" SLOGGING " BIRMINGHAM "SLOGGERS."

There has lately been an alarming revival of street ruffianism in Birmingham, and a number of private persons have beeh seriously assaulted, especially by gangs of roughs calling themselves " slogging gangs:" An out- cry has been made for heavier sentences on these %Bend- ers, and at the Quarter Sessions,on Tuesday,the Recorder, in two reparate cases, imposed sentences of five years' penal servitude, a third prisoner being sent to eighteen months' hard labour. The Recorder said that unless the spirit of lawlessness was checked, some of the youths of the city would be hanged for murder.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE'S LAND BILL.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S LAND BILL.

A correspondence between Mr. Gladstone and Sir John Colomb appears in the "Daily Telegranh." Mr. Glad- stone writes ;-10, St. James's-square, sth April. Dear sir,—Without entering into details on the subject of your letter, which my time would not permit, I must observe that the policy which the Government of April, 18E6, had resolved on undoubtedly embraced Irish landlords in general. But (1) that policy was not so explained as to reach the sum you describe; (2) the proposal was that contained in the Bill, and the sum asked from Parlia- ment was not £150,000,000, but £50,000,000; (3) it was a proposal made once for all, and on its failure no member of the Government (much less of the party) stood pledged by having made it to its repetition. "The following up," of the offer was entirely contingent on its acceptance, and ended with its failure.—l remain, dear sir, yours very faithfully, W. E. GLansroxc."
MR. PARNELL AND THE IRISH LAND PU RCHA SE BILL

Mr. Parnell, who has given notice of his intention to move the rejection of the Irish Land Bill on its second reading, informed a Central New reporter on Monday night that the measure is perhaps the most serious that has ever been introduced to pledge British credit upon Worthless security. The hon. gentleman said : "It makes a very big dip into the pockets of the British tax- payers,startmg as it does with a demand for £33,000,000, to which £10,000,000 will have to be added. In return for this the Act would draw in only the insolvent tenants and those landlords who desire to rid themselves of impoverished and worthless properties. The result of such a state of things would be that we should acquire unsaleable estates, forming a completely worthless security." Questioned as to his health, Mr. Parnell stated that he is much stronger now.

SATURDAY, APRIL 19, 1890.

Factory Loan Cnoss as Secretary of State Labour in for India is likely to get himself in s trouble and be the cause of no i.,111411 Mischief, if he does not act justly and firmly cit tile matter of legislation for our great Depen- f_encY• His India Councils Bill is conceived and vu,ttaed in such a narrow spirit that already, in :1093 parts of the country, protests are being .ited against it. What the people want is some arl/5":1 of elective representation. Their demands modest and reasonable, and they ought to be r"eded• Another matter which is exciting atten- th is „a hill which is under the consideration of ,Dl.v jeerers Council for the amendment of the ti 7,14 raetory Act. The millowners who are on PM are doing all they can to prevent any er restriction of the hours of labour of women taucatki children, and the usual nonsense is being ea about ruining manufacturers, and driving Cue out of the country—just as it was in Eng- -2,4 When Lord SHAFTESBURY began his work of "aorta of our own factory system. There is a 13°Int in restriction, of course, which would result , in i . taaging the cotton trade in India; but it s ,',-"calous to talk of any approach to that point India and England are on a like footing with gatd to hours of labour. Production in the Rettell • t i radO n this countr,y wile never greater v`'llah it is at this moment and the hours of labour z:te never less. Increased speed, improved 119er1, and better processes have more than BUp for the temporary drawback sustained by 'l4lleing the working hours. And it will be the lianle in India, if the Government will be firm, and teatrict the labour of women and children to the 44tale hours that are worked in this country. 'Unfortunately the bill as it stands doee not go far enough ; and yet the millowners of India are t,l:Ylng to cripple it. They plead that" the mild 4iedoo " is anxious that his children should work at the factory, and urge that he would not think ..°„f 'Rich a thing if the hours of labour were in- llitkals to health. But that is no argument at all, Ithere would have been no need for Factory tocte in this country ; and it is a matter of course eay that there is in all probability an average 949ount of human nature in the composition of " the mild Hindoo." But the best answer to Vect 18.1 pleading of, this kind is to be found in the tZl3°lts of medical and non-medical officials, and eY Ilbew conclusively that native children are as rule weak, stunted, miserable creatures. How °milt be otherwise, working as they do, year in kltal: Year out, about 80 hours per week, and with t.._tet9Perature in hot weather fluctuating be- ,""en 110 and 120 degrees in the shade ! They gunday, too—shame on us, for we are all rti°te or less responsible in the iniquity, so long as India cotton mills are permitted to proceed 09 their ever lasting grind. It is true that xr Ilays are granted on certain Hindu and all°9ledan festivals; but, as these occur about a ,il.74ea days in the year only, it is a fraud to set ~...7'et° up as a substitute for fifty-two Sundays. It -44t1sfactory to see that, in the Amendment Bill, • Wen is made for four days' holiday in a month OUivalent, that is to say, to a Sunda; stoppage ngland; but on the other hand it is altogether C.2a_ tisfactory to observe that the hours of labour tZ women and children will still be a great deal tv,l(4lfl• For instance, children between nine and thre,years of age will be required to work sixty- hoZte hours per week, that is, six-and-a-half longer than men in the factories at home. totather, females of twelve and upwards will have 6.:?..ca'k eleven hours per day, or some twenty hours 47,er than adult males work in England. Will r-m Caess say this is fair to the natives of nttip And if it is not fair, what is he tetui --'retary of State for India going to do in order set this crooked thing straight ? It is no use sending delegates to Labour Conferences at i te YIP and posing as the pioneers of protection °4len and children in England, if at the same wOS allow the women and children of India to re ,„"bed by ill-conceived and barbarous factory vclnTatiens. What has/proved good for England Prcrire good for India, if fair trial be made. ,--cus dear the air of cant, and deal justly with e °ver-wrought factory operatives in our far- -4°4Y Dependency.

TEE HOME SECRETARY made ,an puneltisPiainitaeltit. explanation in the House of Com- mons, on Monday, as to his reason for haextending mercy to one of the Crewe murderers, 4,0-I;4_ denYing it to the other. It would seem that, 17"4ough both lads were under nineteen, it was Zeallse George was two years younger than chard that he got the benefit of the i recommend- toite;:litig e! the jury. The explanation explains for there is nothing to suggest, as was aerned probable, that Mr. MATTHEWS has been I),t in possession of additional information to that before the public at the trial. The blundering r °ill° Secretary ht.is callously disregarded the ,eecltatnendation of the jury, which applied equally both culprits, and he has outraged public opinion ,43711.8h°14'ing mercy to one youth and hanging the r_,' We do not profess to say that the recona- -'n'uation of a jury is in all cases to be treated as BGmethingsaered; but it is a starting point for the 11°/neSecretsry,and it ought not to he disregarded except for reasons which will stand criticism. If the •ews Of jurymen are to be treated as of little or no juries will be tempted to protect thern-.' selves _ by ref usinf, t) bring in verdicts of " guilty" it is a ease of murder under extenuating'

circumstances. Already the brutal miscarriage of justice which has occurred, has turned the minds of the multitude to the old question as to whether it is really desirable in any case to take the life of a citizen as ft penalty for wrong-doing. It is nothing to the purpose to quote the old injunction —an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, and a life for a life. We have, it is to be hoped, got beyond the rude ideas of justice which were prevalent three thousand years ago. Society does not, or should not, punikfli now-a-days in order to satisfy a desire for vengeance. Punishment is unwarrant- able except with two, or one of two, objects in view, namely, the amendment of the criminal, and the protection of the community, by deterring other offenders. It is obvious that when a criminal is put out of existence he is beyond the reach of amendment in this world, and that so far as he is concerned one of the main objects of punishment is disregarded. What is left to con- sider is whether capital punishment is absolutely necessary for the safety of society. For ourselves we do not profess to have any confident opinion upon the subject; but we should like to see the experiment made of abolishing the death penalty for a number of years. It would then be observed vvhether the murderer, with the fear of death no longer before his eyes, would be more active in his operations; and, if it was found that life was taken more recklessly, it would be a simple matter to set the hangman to work again. We dismiss as a childish fear the idea that a large crop of mur- derers would instantly arise, if, capital punish- ment were abolithed. It was found that the fear of death did not deter people from stealing in the old, bad days, when theft was punishable with death. The knowledge that a more merciful code has not resulted in an increase of crime ought to encourage us in saying—we will try if we cannot keep society stable without, when one life is lost, trying to mend matters by destroying another. And beyond this broad view of the subject, there is the awful consideration that juries now and again make mistakes, and men are hanged who are really' innocent. RICHARD DAVIES went on the scaffold protesting that he had no part in the actual murd- er of his father, and WILLIAM CHADWICK, who was hanged on Tuesday, asserted up to the last that he was not guilty of the Atherton crime. The chance that either Devras or CHADWICK Woke the truth is, it may be granted, a slender one; but it is a chance; and it is not agreeable to reflect that whatever facts may be brought to light hereafter the execution of these men renders it impossible that they should benefit by them. Look at the subject from any and every point of view, it will be perceived that there is much to be said in favour of thv gxpegiragatal abolition of capital punish- ment.
M. Gosonzx as Chancellor of the The Budget. Exchequer submitted his Midget to

the House of Commons, on Thurs- day evening. He had, as was anticipated, a sur- plus of over three millions ; and he has disposed of it in a manner which is on the whole fairly satis- factory. There is to be a reduction of 2d. in the lb. on the tea duty; and a reduction of the duty on currants of ss. per cwt. The sum of £lOO,OOO is to be set aside for the better equipment of the Volunteers, and the tax on inhabited houses is to be reduced on houses with a rental between £2O and £6O per year. Besides this, there is to be a remission of the duty upon gold and silver plate. ' The income-tax is,. however, left untouched, ' although it is a war-tax Which continuos to be kept lup in time of peace; and there is nothing at all done in the direction of carrying out Lord SALIS- BURY'S qualified promise to make education free. It is by no means creditable to us as a nation that the bulk of the surplus—£l,Boo,ooo—has been realised through an extraordinary increase in the consumption of intoxicating liquors. There has been a rush upon spirits—and particularly upon ruin. We agree with the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer in saying the result is one to be deplored, that it is a matter to be looked fairly in the face, and that it "places upon the Government and upon the House an increasing liability to deal with the question of the consumption of alcoholic drinks" Mr. GOSCHEN has taken action to the extent of putting sixpence per gallon upon British and foreign spirits. This is good as far as it goes, for it is in accord with the sound maxim that it is wise to tax the luxuries rather than the neces- saries of life. It is also proposed that there shall be a suspension of the issue of new licenses until the licensing question has been dealt with as a whole. This is not much; but then there is nothing great about the Budget, and we must be thankful for small mercies when the Tories are in power.

They have just dug out another "dug-out" in the track of the Ship Canal. What next? Is there any likelihood of the diggers finding a " dugger "?

The portraits of General Von capriiri, the new German Chancellor, indicate a man not' unlike Bismarck in strength of character; but with an altogether more genial look. "Blood and Iron" is all very well now and again, but people prefer in the long run the milk of' human kindness.

The evidence accumulat es that Prince Bismarck's retirement is in the nature of a fall. It is not long since the Emperor William said :—" All who assist me in my great task I shall heartily welcome, but those who oppose me in this work I shall crush." This is the sort of game that Bismarck has hitherto had all to himself. Can it be that he retires in order that he may not, in the end, be a victim of the crash?

"At Burnley, on Monday, a factory opemtive named Boardman was remanded charged with breaking and entering a vault at Holy Trinity Church, whilst under the influence of drink." Boardman seems to have snade a little mistake. There are vaults and vaults- Can he have been "blind drunk"?

The incident is a reminder of the city church, under a corner of which them was a vault for the storage of spirits. The conjunction of the two so tickled the fancy of a wag, that he pinned the following on the door of the storehouse : There 's a spirit above and a spirit below— A spirit of bliss and a spirit of woe. The spirit above is the spirit Divine, But the spirit below is the spirit of wine.

The nation ITeathes freely again. The Duke of Cambridge has made it known that, " so long as he has health and strength to do his; duty," he does not mean to resign his post as Commander-in- chief. This being the case—and as age is no dis- qualification—he will doubtless for a long time have health and strength to do his duty, and draw his salary.
According to the "Review of Reviews "--" The Czar is a steady, cautions man, with a passionate horror of war, and a supreme sense of his respon- sibility for the maintenance of peace." This is

SWINE FEVER IN RiIISCORN DISTRICT.

John Goff and Peter Itadley., old men, who live in Holloway, were each summoned to Runcorn Police Court, to answer a charge of being in possession of four pigs, which were affected with swine fever, end neglecting to 'give notice to the police authorities. Inspector Bowyer said on the 7th inst. he visited the premises of the defend- ants. In their respective pig-styes he found three pigs suffering from swine fever, and in an adjoining field he discovered two pigs burieid, one belonging to each defend- ant. Mrs. Goff admitted that the pigs were unwell, and she had not reported the matter to save other people, who had told her to keep it quiet. Mr Ferguson, veter- ,ittaxv surgeon, said he made a post-mortem examination of tle dead pigs on the following day. They had both suffered from swine fever,. The remaining pigs were also txiffering from the disease, and had done so for about 14 days. Each defendant was ordered to pay El, including costs, amounting to ifs. 9d. DEFRACDING THE L. AND N.-W. RAILWAY CONSTANT, AT WIDNES.

• On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions,Thos. Roberts, r labourer, of Crouton, was charged with having, on the ! Ist March, travelled on the London and North-Western ! Hallway Co. without ticket, with intent to defraud. On ! the day named, the defendant arrived at Ditton by the 7-5 p.m. Manchester train, and instead of passing over 'tke bridge, he crossed the line. A porter named George Taylor watched him, and saw him enter the engine house. He followed, and defendant, in reply to his ques- tions, said he had come by train, and had given up his ticket to a porter on the platform. Taylor said he wAs the only porter on the platform, and the defendant then offered to pax his fare from Rainhill. The defend- ant was under the influence of Mink at the time. A fine of 20s. ;-,ml costs was imposed.—George Grice, of 90, chureh-st., Farnworth, was summoned for riding from Helsby to,Ditton, without ticket, on the Bth Mai ch. The defendant said he had forgotten to get his ticket, and was sorry tm, what he had done.--Be was fined 20s. and Costs. •

Faith in immortality was surely never more con- fidently expressed than in the following observa- tion made by the late Robert Browning :---" Death, death, it is thisharping on death that I despise so much. Without death, which is our crapelike, churchyardy word for change, there could be no prolongation of that which we call life. For my- self, I deny death as the end of everything. Never say of me that I am dead."

The Germans in Canada have been taking the trouble to suggest to the Emperor of Germany that it is very undesirable that the German Jesuits in the New World should be permitted to return to the Fatherland? It is very good of them to do this, though it does seem a little odd that, if they dislike the Jesuits so much, they should want to keep them a.nongst them in America. Can it be that, while their dislike of the Jesuits is great, their love of Fatherland is greater?

Referring to the Irish Land Bill of the Govern- ment, and the opposition to Home Rule,the "Star" thus neatly hits off the inconsistency of the Tories: —" The Irish are good enough to borrow our money, but they are not good enough to manage their own affairs—including the distribution of their own money. It requires a Tory mind to dis- cover why it is that a man can be so dishonest as not to be trusted with his own purse, and so honest as to be perfectly safe as a custodian of the4mrse of somebody else."

The" Daily Islt,ws " says :—" Strong pressure is being put upon the Government in the interests of the Church party to direct that in the Census to be taken next year the public shall be required to enter the religious denomination under which they range themselves." Churchmen no doubt think that such a course would enable them to make a good show. And it would ; for the outsiders will put themselves down as " Church." But what matters? The Disestablishment movement is not going to be staved off by a census.

A contemporary says :—"The secretary of the Bishop of Alalta has arrived in Rome for the our- pose of receiving instructions from the Vatican relative to the understanding between the Holy See and Great Britain just concluded by Sir J. L. Simmons." Now, what is "the understanding? " If Mr. Gladstone had been in office, Orangemen would have made the welkin ring with cries of "No Popery." Perhaps Mr. John Roberts, as an Orangeman will explain when he addresses the electors of North West Ward why this is thus.

-- At the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, a man named Hampson was mulcted in a penalty. of 245. for "having his house in a filthy condition, injurious to health." Judging from the evidence, there could be no question as to the abominable condition of the house, and, as the defendant had previously been warned, he well deserved to be punished. But 245. is.a large sum' to a man who earns, according to his statement, little more than that in a fortnight. It would be in every way more satisfactory to have more frequent cases,and lighter penalties.

-- Mr. T. W. Leith addressed his cOnstituents at Newton, on Saturday. He is reported to have said :—" It had begun to dawn upon most people, and also upon the minds of their opponents, that the question of Home Rule was beginning to fall very flat • it was a hitter pill which was being ad- ministered to the British public, and it required considerable gilding." There seems to have been a little mistake. It must have been the Irish Land Bill he was referring to. That pill does re- quire "considerable gilding," and it has not gone down yet.

The movement for the extension of the War- rington Infirmary is going with something like a rush. Alderman Davies, in presiding over tho meeting, held on Monday, made a statement which constituted a really powerful appeal, and it is meeting with a generous response. Already over £2,500 have been promised, and there is no reason why £4,000 should not be raised. This would enable the Committee to complete the work in first-class style, and leave a balance in hand for contingencies. The task is worth doing, and it is worth doing well.

A correspondent in a contemporary, referring to the absurd statements made by Mr. Chamberlain and others as to Mr. Gladstone's " change of front before the election of 1885," furnishes a refu- tation by quoting the speech of Lord Hartington at the Eighty Club, in March 1886, as follows : I am not going to say one word of complaint or charge against Mr. Gladstone for the attitude which he has taken on this question. I think no one who has read or heard, daring along ser.es of years, the declarations of Mr. Gladstone on the question of self-government for Ireland can be surprised at the tone of his present declarations. . . . When I look back to those declarations that Mr. Gladstone made in Parliament, which have not been unfre- quent ; when I look back to the increased definite- ness given to those declarations in his address to the electors of Midlothian, and in his Midlothian speeches ; I say, when I consider these things, I feel that I have not, and that no one has, any right to complain of the tone of the declarations which Mr. Gladstone has recently made upon his subject." What has Mr. Chamberlain to say to this? He calls Lord Hartington his leader, does he not?

At Widn-as Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Patrick Devereaux • wassummoned for wounding a carrier pigeon. the property of Wm. Jones. On the sth inst Mrs. Jones was in the kitchen and noticed the bird to fall to the ground. She went outside and saw the defendant with a catapult in his hand. His relations had since tried to settle the case. The complainant said the bird was worth £5 and was damaged to the extent of 10s. to £1 by hay- ing one of its wings broken. The defendant did not appear and he was fined ss. and costs and ordered to pay 6s. 6d. damage. SPRING Fesnroas. Spring Fssiliofls.. & W. DUTTON. 16 and 18, Sankey-st., Warrington.--.Adrt. ' _

Maitland Wood, M.A., vicar of Runcorn, and in the evening by the Rev. F. W. Willis, M.A., rector of Warrington. Both services were very successful. The numerical returns presented to the quarterly meeting of the St. Helens and Prescot Circuit recently held, showed a membership of 1,154—a decrease of 27 for the year. The financial condition of the circuit was reported to be healthy. The Revs., W. W.' Spencer, A. P. Watson, and G. Hammond were cordially invited to remain a thud year, and the Rev. J. T. Wardle Stafford invited to the circuit from the ensuing conference in succession to the Rev. Thomas Jackson. Three gentlemen celebrated their Jubilee as local preachers, Mr. Armistead, Dr. McNicoll, and Mr. Hewitt, and were thanked for their fifty years valuable services.—The total membership of the Liverpool District is 20,551, a net decrease of 284. St. Helens and Pieslot circuit is the largest in the district in point of numbers, while the number in junior classes exceeds that of ally often EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Z should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Onion, American. and other fines.— John Walker, agent, " Examiner ' Office, Horsey-a.. div.p: "BONA FIDE TRAVELLERS" AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions. on Monday, James Hudson and Edgar Worth,members of O'Beirne's Opera Company, were summoned for having falsely represented them- selves to he travellers and attempted to obtain beer at the Castle Hotel, Halton, during prohibited hours. Mr. Burton represented the defendants, who did not appear, and pleaded guilty. On Good Friday the defendants went to the Castle Hotel, stated they had come from Manchester, and ordered two glasses of beer. P.C. Fryer discovered thatthey had slept in Runcorn on the previous evening, and prevented the landlady supplying the liquor. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed.

div.head: THIBSTT_THIRF AT Ti TON.
div.p: A THIBSTT_THIRF AT Ti TON.

At the Widnes- Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs. F. H. Gossage and Major Gasket!, Thomas Burns, Lugs- dale-road. and Charles White, 4, Widnes-road, were each charged with stealing a bottle containing a pint of beer from the person of Joseph Roberts, on the 13th inst., valued at 30. Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared on behalf of the defendants.—The prosecutor stated that he was a labourer, and lived in Halewood-road, Ditton. He was in the New Inn, Ditton, a few minutes before ten o'clock on Sunday night, and whilst at the bar the two defen- dants passed him. He then missed the bottle of beer from his pocket, and followed the defendants outside, when he asked Burns for it back again or its value. Burns then handed the bottle over to White and they both went away in the direction of Ditton Chapel, and took the bottle with them. He then came across P.C. Townley, and they both went back in search of the prisoners. Subsequently they found the bottle of beer produced in the ditch.—On being charged Burns pleaded guilty, and having been sworn said he passed the bottle to a man named Dunn and not to the prisoner White. White knew nothing about the beer.—The Chairman said they did not think there was sufficient evidence against White, and ho would be discharged. Burns would be fined 21. RErasralc GRA.TIM—J. S. Garland, 51, Lir:age-street, War rington.

div.head: RETIREMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT JOHNSTON. _ .
div.p: RETIREMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT JOHNSTON. _ .

...- Mr. Superintendent Johnston, of the Widnes Police Force, has sent in his resignation to the Lancashire County Council. Mr. Johnston has completed almost 25 years' service, and is therefore, entitled to a pension. The superintendent, who is by birth an Irishman, entered the force in 1865 at Preston, and served as a constable at Old Swan, Aigburth. and Garston. In 1877, Mr. John-. ston was promoted to the rank of inspector. Two years later, while at Gaiston, he was further promoted to the rank of superintendent and removed to St. Helens. Here Mr. Johnston remained until the Ist of duly, 1887, when the Corporation of St. Helens established a borough police force. He was then removed to Widnes, where he has since remained. The people of Widnes have expressed regret that Superintendent Johnston has decided to re- tire after nearly 25 years' service. During the three years he has had control of the local force, Mr. Johnston has on the respect and esteem of the inhabitants, by the kindliness of his disposition, and his courteous bear- ing, whilst carrying out duties, often of an unpleasant nature, and his subordinates have for him the warmest admiration.

A BUTCHER'S WAGER AT RUNCORN AND ITS RESULT. On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Geo. Slater, butcher, High-st., was summoned for assaulting Tom Clough, butcher's assistant, Prineess-st. A cross-sum- mons was issued by Slater, charging Clough with assault- ing him.—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys represented Clough. It was alleged, on behalf of Cough, that on the night of the 2nd April, shortly after eleven o'clock, he was on his way home when he saw a man on the ledge of the window of his cousin's shop in Church-st. Two other men were standing on the parapet. He inquired what they were doing there, and Slater, who was on the ledge, asked what businets it was of his. There was "sundry language" used and Slater then struck Clough twice with his fist, once on the ear and once on the face causing considerable bruise and swelling. On 'the other side it was contended that Clough trade use of much bad language, and struck first at Slater who warded off the blow and hit his assailant tviioe. In cross-examinationby Mr. Humphreys, it transpired that Slater and two other butchers named Spencer and Thomas, ha e 'made a wager with respect to the weight of a beast in Thomas Clough's shop in Church-st., and they were endeavouring to look inside thenhop, when the complainant Clough appeared on the scene. After hear- ing the evidence, the Bench dismissed both sammonses. Mr. Humphrey pointed out that Skater bad admitted the assault and in justice to his client, he Mt boned to pro- test against the dismissal of a defentia,ut who bad prac- tically pleaded guilty. RUNCORN PARI43II cauitca NESTRY. The annual vestry meeting in connection with RilnCtirti Parish Church was held on Fniday night last week il4 Bethesda Lecture Nall. The Rev. A. M Wood, vicar, presided and there was a goad attend- ance iliauding a numbenof Nonconformi•ta. At tlie outset I he Chairman explained the reason why the meeting was held in that room, instead of in the National Schools which they had found convenient enot4l in the, past. Re ',rated that he was not aware until recently,that Runcorn in 1,880 was placed under the Act for the preven- tion of holding Vestries in Churches, and Mr. Sutton had brought the notice printed in the " Gazette." That room, by some agreement made at that time, became the vestry room and as far as he could understand since that time it had been necessary to, hold all vestry meetings there. Ile had no doubt there were good grounds for not holding the meetings them that had been held elsewhere, but it was always well to be on the right side and inasmuch as it waklearly legal to hold the vestry meeting there, and it was net clearly legal to hold it elsewhere, it was thought advisable to put themselves right and come into that room. They would not present anyaccounts to that meeting because the vestry found no money and did not rate or tax the population of the town for the support of , the church. The accounts were made up of voluntary gifts of the worshippers of the Church at Etuncoria, so that they were not subject to the revision of the vestry and nonsiderable inconvenience might arise if it were es-

tablished as a precedent that the private accounts of the Church and the gifts which were made during divine service were to be overlooked and perhaps voted upon by a meeting which would consist of any ratepayer of the town. That bring so they would all perceive that it was inadvisable to submit,' formally at any rate, the accounts to that meeting.

THE CHARITIESt The Chairman said he had received from Mr. Sutton a diPpy of a resolution passed at a vestry meeting a week or two previously, asking that the charity accounts should be presented at the next vestry meeting. That was the next meeting, and so he felt it to be his duty to say what he had to say there. The Vicar then placed on the table the accounts of the Alcock, the Rigby, and the Organ Fund. The churchwardens had not received any accounts of the Liptrot Charity, the trustees of which considered that they did not come under the Act, and were not, therefore, bound to present accounts annually; but the treasurer, Mr. W. Fisher, would permit any ratepayer who liked to see the accounts. The par- ticulars of the accounts are as follows :—Rigby Charity, the sum of £l5 supplied by Mr. W. E. Rigby, as a year's interest on £3OO held by him as surviving trustee ot the will of Josiah •Rigby, deceased. The charity was distri- buted on All Saints' Day as follows :-61 petticoats (244 yards of flannel, at• 13d.), £l3 4s. 4d. ' • making of the petticoats at sd. each, £1 ss. sd. ; calico and tape, 7s. 9d. ; tickets, 2s. 6d. ; total £l5. Alcock Charity, Dividends from consols, £6 is. Bd. MR. DIRGES OBJECTS TO BETHESDA HALL. Mr. Digges said he had a great objection to meeting in that room, and a great number of parishioners had die same objection, and as it all emanated from one source that they were meeting there and he thought they ought to be enlighted why they were compelled to meet there. (Applause.)—Mr. Sutton said the town's meeting for merly was held in the cffice in Alcock-st., and on many occasions ratepayers were standinz half way across the street. Then the order referred to by the Vicar was obtained.—Mr. Digges: You say town's meeting. I mean vestry ineetim.T. —Mr. Sutton: That is the vestrymeeting. There is only one vestry.—Mr. Digges: I call that last week the town's meeting.—Mr. Sutton : It is the vestry meeting. Ile explained that he was parish clerk when the order was obtained and the Vicar was consulted. The Betties la Lecture Hall was the only room where they could get which would fulfil the condition of the Local Government Board. That room was lease for a term of 14 years at the rate of 15s. per meeting. The lease had fouryears to run.—Mr. Digges : Is there a penalty for meeting elsewhere.--Mr. Sutton : I don't know that there is any penalty. It is the hands of the Vicar.—Mr. Digges: I tnoNi, that we adjourn to the National Schools. —The Chairman said the only objection was that it was possible that the proceedings might not be legal if they did.—A parishioner said it did not make any difference where the meeting was held.—Mr. Digges said outsiders could come to that room they would not go to the schoolroom ; there were one or two in that room who were not regular ;Menders at the Parish Church, and he thought that it was unfair that these outsiders should take part in the business .1 the Parish Church. They did not go to other churches and take part in their work. Mr. Digges motion was not seconded and the business was proceeded with. -

THE BELLRINSERS AND THEIR PAY. Mr. Joynson and several other bellringers demanded to be paid six months' salary amounting to £5 for ringing the bells at the Parish Church.—Mr. Marwood said the money had always previously It:wn voted at the vestry meeting: but no vote was given last year, and the rinr.ers were not engaged to ring. The ringers had said they were determined to have certain terms or they, would stop ringing, and they were told they could stop if they liked. They would have been paid but they were too lazy to collect their gratuities. and wanted the wardens to collect them.—A Ringer: We were not too lazy, but the parishioners did not wish us to do it.—Mr. Marwood said he had it in black and white that they were too lazy.—A ringer demanded that the written statement should be produced.—Mr. Marwood.said the ringers had left in such a manner that the Church Coun- cil did not think they were entitled to any salary.— Several ringers said they were legally entitled to pay- ment and the matter dropped. div.head: SHOCKING HOVELS AT RUNCORN„
div.p: SHOCKING HOVELS AT RUNCORN„

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas, James Griffiths was summoned under the Public! Health Act., 1875, that-the cottage occupied by him was over-crowded so as to be dangerous or injurious to the health of the inmates.—Mr. F. A. Lake prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Commissioners, and said the defend ant occupied a cottage in Law's Court, off Cooper- street. The cottage consisted of a stnall living room with a bedroom above. The, inmates were the de- fendant and his wife, ason and his wife and a child. The cubic capacity of the house was 1.121 feet, and accord- ing to the Act 300 feet was the lowest space allowed for , one person.—The defendant said his son and daughter- in-law could notget a house, and they were living there luntil they did 80. He could not turn them out. He admitted that he had received notice to abate the nuis- ance.—The Bench made an order upon the defendant to abate the nuisance in a week and pay costs.—Abraham Hampson, 811 old man, of 15, Zion Place, was brought up uncier asi milarsum mons, and he was further charged with having the premises in such a ethv state as to be injuri- ous to the health of the inhabitants.—Mr. Lake said the defendant occupied a house in a court sometimes known as the Del ph Hole, more generally as Zion Place. The Ceturt con4sted of an old emarry, the side of which formed the back walls of the houses. The defendant's Muse consisted of a small room downstairs, and a bed- room. The bedroom was *occupied by the defendant and his wife, his son aged 23 nd a daughter 18 years. The cubic area was 877 feet and there ought to ' be 1.200 made feet for four persons. A serious item in 'connection with this house was its filthy erudition. It , had apparently not been cleaned for months or years and was thick with filth. The only ornamentation on the wallsseemed to be the•excreta of the pests with which the h DUSC was infested. The defendant had been repea- tedly warned. Mr. Percival, inspector of nuisances, mid it was the most filthy house he had ever been in during his fife. It was-scarcely possible to get upstairs or old rags and other nebbish. In the bed room there . was a bad on the floor, and in one corner two bags of • dlittfl. Dr. Spear, an iwsttector of the Local Government Board, would not enterthe house because oh its filthiness. There wagamly sufficient cubic area in the house to .aecornmodate two pertalns.—The Bench ordered the defendant to reduce the number of inmates to two within a week, and havethe place cleaned within three days ; also to pay the costs 255, or to go to gaol for 14 •I dart.—The defendant said he would go to gaol.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL- BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL- BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday. Mr. H. Wade-Deacon presided and there were present the Rev. Dean Finegan, Major Wareing, Messrs. Barlow, Brown, and Quinn, and G. H. Danby (clerk.)

div.head: INCREASE OF SALARIES.
div.p: INCREASE OF SALARIES.

On the proposition of Dean Finegan it was resolved that when the question of an increase of salary to an officer or servant of the Board is to he considered at any Committee meeting, notice of the proposed increase be entered upon the summons sent to each member of such Committee. On the recommendation of the General Purposes Committee the salary of Mr. Walter Peacock be increased £l5 per annum.

DISTRICT EDI7CATION. The District Education Committee reported that during March there were 246 applications for school fees, which were recommended to he paid in 244 cases. 260 persons were summoned before the Committee for Contravention of the Education Act, and 26 were prosecuted and 25 convicted by the magistrates. One boy was sent to a truant school.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.,
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.,

The School Management Committee recommended that Charles William Stuart be engaged as monitor, in the senior boys department of Simms Cross School, at the rate of 10s. per month. That Miss Lilly Mercer be en- gaged as assistant mistress in the infants department of Simms Cross Schools' at a salary of 355. per annum, rising according to the scale of the Board. The Com- mittee reported that they had arranged that the holidays at the schools this year should be as follows :—Whit week and three weeks at midsummer, commencing at noon on Friday June 27th, and ending on the morning of Monday July 21st, 1890. The minute re-holidays was referred back to the Committee, so that they might ar- range the holidays in uniformity with theholidays of the denominational schools.
FINANCE.

The Finance Committee reported the payment of ac- counts amounting to £598 10s. 46. The receipts Ter the mouth amounted to £143 15s. 91 The Finance Com- mittee submitted the financial statement for tte half year ceded the 25th March, 1890. Thereceipts amounted to £4,463 12s. 81, and included a balance of £579 9s. 7d. from last half year; grants from the Committee of Coun- cil on Education, including grants from the Science and Art Departtn?nt, £2,927 14s. 4d.: school fees, £9ll 178.104. ; books and other articles sold to children, £l3 55., 7d. div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. JOHN
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MR. JOHN
lIIITCHISON.

On Tuesday afternoon the remains of the late Mr. John Hutchison, inspector for Parr's Banking Company, Limited, were interred in St. Penni churchyaid, Warrington. Mr. Hutchison's death took place very suddenly yesterday afternoon week. He was at Chester station about half-past three in the afternoon, waiting for the 3.45 train for War- rington, when lie suddenly fell forward on his face. He was at once raised from the ground, but it was found that death had apparently been instantaneons. Mr. Hutchison, who was 69 years of age, was originally in the service of Messrs. Parr. Lyon and Co., and when this Arm was converted into Parr's Banking Company, Limited, he still continued in its employ. At one time he was manager of the Company's Runcorn branch, but having resigned this position on account of ill-health he was appointed inspector of the branch establishments. The deceased gentleman was the author of a work on "The Practice of Banking," three volumes of which have been published, the fourth passing through the press at tile time of Mr. Hutchison's death. He leaves three sons and one daughter. The Rev. Ernest Hutchison, of South Lambeth, London, is the eldest son; the second son, George, is engaged in a bank at Kimberley, South Africa; and the third is an articled pupil in an advocate's office in Edinburgh. The funeral, as we have stated, took place on Tuesday. The mourners were the Rev. Ernest Hutchison (son of tho deceased), Mr. Geo. Hutchison (son), Miss Hutchison (daughter), Mr. J. B. Wright, London (uncle), Mr. Rich.. Kent, Master Elwood Kent, Mr. C. Sawkins Burgess, Mr.. J. Mathers, (Southport), Mr. Stanhouse, Mr. Laret Burn, Dr. White (deceased's medical attendant), Mr. W. D. Jeans (family solicitor), aid Mrs. Bettaley. Parr)! Banking Company were represented by Mr. Wm. Silcock, Mr. McGregor, and Mr. F. Farrington, of Wigan. The Rev. S. Wilkinson was the officiating clergyman, The coffin, which was made in Chester. was of polished oak„ with brass mountings, and on a brass plate was the in- scription—" John Hutchison, died April 11, aged 67, years." The funeral arrangements were carried out by - Mr. W. C. Nicholson, on behalf of Messrs. R. Garnett and Sons, of Warrington. A number of beautiful wreaths. had been forwarded by sorrowing friends and relatives,, including one from the Warrington Bank, and one eacb_i from the Wigan and Chester Branches.

CONVBRSION INTO A PUBLIC COMPANY. It will be seen from the 'prospectus printed in our advertising columns that the old established breweries and businesses of Peter Walker and Son, carried on by Sir Andrew 11. Walker, Bart., have been converted into a public bompany, and will be registered under the name of Peter Walker and Son, Warrington and Burtou.Lirnited. The company is largely a Liverpool undertaking, and has been formed wittuort the assistance of any financiers or other interme-- diaries, itad freed from the payment of promotion money- or other charges frequently incurred in the formstionor public nom panics. In addition to the or(linary shares, which ainount to £1,000,000 sterling, and which are held by the vendor, Sir. A. B. Walker, a nd his nominees, there- are 100,000 preference shares of £lO each, and £1,000,000 of debentures in multiples of £lOO. Of both debentures and preference shares Sir A. It. Walker retains a third,. and the remainder are offered' to the. public. The debentures are at 4 per cent., and the preference shares. hear a cumulative preferential dividend or 5 per cent. The brokers in Liverpool are Messrs. %%Irma% Chambres and Company, Dale-st., and the solicitors are Messrs. j Miller, Peel, Hughes, and Company, of Cosk-st., Liver— pool. div.head: SUPPOSED WHOLESALE SUICILSE
div.p: SUPPOSED WHOLESALE SUICILSE

A sensational case of supposed wholesale suicide, by poisoning and suffocation, is reported from Moscow, where, in one of the rooms occupied by a widow, her five daughters were found suffocated by charcoal fumes. In another apartment lay a large number of dead cats and dogs, and in a third room the mother was found poisoned, her death apparently dating from some days pre- viously.

div.head: . BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: . BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

. GOING TO THE BRIDEWELL FOR A BED. James Murphy came before the Warrinzton magis- trates en. Wednesday, on a charge of drunkenness. On Tuesday night he walked into the Parade-room at the Bridewell, and lay down on a brim ConstabitJones 43) went to him, and Murphy said he wanted to gl to sleep. The Constable told him he was in the wrong place, and sent him away, but prisoner returned, and rested himself -on the footpath. He was thereupon locked up. A fine of 53. and costs was imposed.

div.head: OVBEICROWDED AND DIRTY.
div.p: OVBEICROWDED AND DIRTY.

At V7arringtOn Police Court, on Monday, Michael Craghan, Alorris'-yard, Silver-street, was summoned for keeping an unregistered and insanitary lodging-house. Inspector Powell said he visited the house on the Bth April, and found in it eleven persons, six of whom were lodgers. The place was adapted for four only. In- spector Norman said that the 'dirty state of the bedding and everything in the house was beyond description. A penalty of 10s. and costs was imposed in respect to the first charge. The second case was adjourned for a fort- night.
DRINK A.ND VIOLENCU.

On Tuesday, at the Warrington Police Court, a painter named John Stirrup, who lives in Winwick-road, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on Town-hill, on Monday, and with having assaulted P.C. Clough at the same time and place. That officer saw prisoner drunk and begging in Lyme-et. He began to assist him on his way home, but before they had gone many steps the prisoner struck him a violent blow in the face. He was then taken into custody. On the way to the Station he assaulted the officer again, knocking him down and kicking him several times. With the assistance of P.C. Wood, prisoner was conveyed to the Bridewell. The Bench imposed a fine of 10s. and costs.
NEWSPAPER HAWKING IN THE STREETS.

A man named James Mullins was summoned to the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, for having per- mitted his son, a boy seven years of age, to sell news- papers, contrary to the bye-la Ns. The case was proved by a constable,who said that at twenty minutes past ten on the night of the 9th inst., he ll'aS in Sankey-at., when he saw the boy Mullins shouting newspapers for sale. It was a very wet, cold night, and there were scarcely any people about. The boy was with a brother, who was 13 years old. Defendant's wife said that the elder brother took the little one to sell papers without her knowledge.- The Chief Constable observed that shout- ing and bawling in the streets was getting as bad as ever. Shlekeepers in the main streets complained very much of it. Defendant was ordered to pay costs, 3s. 6d.
ANOTHER SCIZIMIL OF BAD FISK.

The Warrington magistrates. on Monday, had a case before them, in which Sarah Ihlittall, 6, Crowther-st., Manchester, was summoned for having had in her pos- sesion. on the 3rd April, intended for sale, 130Ibs. of cod- fish, 181bs. of coal fish, 21bs. of ray; and 12lbs. of her- rings. which were unfit for human food. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), who prosecuted, said that on the 2nd April Inspector Norman found a quantity of fish at the Central Station, and subsequently watched the trains. On the following day he saw the defendant alight from the 11.9 a.mArain and take possession of the fish, the greater portion of which was in a 'ox. :Being of opinion that the fish was unfit for food, he seized it. It was condemned by the Medical Officer of Health, Dr. Gornall, and subsequently destroyed by order of Mr. Wm. Owen, J.P. Defendant said that she was not going to sell the fish ; she was sending it back as not fit for sale. Mr. Whittle did not press the case unduly, and the Bench cautioned the defendant, and ordered her to pay reduced costs, 15s. 6d.
