div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

. - - MOSS BANK V. Vr,IDNEIS ST. MARY'S.—This return match took place at Moss Bank. The visitors ran,out winners by two goals, four minors, to nil. WYCLIFFS V. Larcaeonn Hoesere.—The first meeting of these teams took place on the ground of the former, en Saturday afternoon, in fine weather, when, after a well contested game, the result was a draw, Wycliffe scoring six minors to Latchford two. The home team had the best of matters, but could not score. In the forward division Wycliffe were superior, but behind the scrimmage the visitors held their own. The following was the Wycliffe team :—Full back, Deakin; three- quarter-backs, Johnson, Cartwright and Brady; half- backs, Noon and Ball ; forward. Lloyd (Captain), Hampson, Gleave, Warburton, Peckham, Ferry, Gaunt, Griffiths, and Barlow. WARRINOTOX " A " v. Rumeeete " A."—The meeting of these local rivals, at Runcorn,on Saturday, has formed the theme of conversation amongst all enthusiasts in the neighbourhood since fixtures were arranged some few weeks back, as the excellent form shown during the season has been noted, and it was a somewhat knotty problem as to which would ultimately claim premier- ship. At the time of starting there was a considerahle number of spectators round the enclosure, and on the teams making their appearance,they Caine in for a round cf applause. Runcorn from the kickoff at once invaded the visitor' quarters, Boscow stopping the rush. The first advantage came to Warrington, however, for after Neild had come from a pack and floored Robinson, a strong rush by Knowles caused Runcorn to line out in their 25. Here a long kick travelled to Jolley, who returned with a hugh punt, and May deemed it expe- dient to touch down. Then Runcorn, taking advantage after charging a kick, broke away to the Warrington quarter, but this was overshadowed by a grand bit of play which followed. Some scrimmaging was taking place when Rowe suddenly stole round a pack, and after getting grandly away, handed to Mather, and the latter throwing quickly to Webster. he by a long kick trans- ferred the game to the home line. Directly afterwards Lees, Barker, and Hughes severely tested Boscow, but 'tie relieved, and Rowe supplemented this by another smart run. This was succeeded by scrimmages, but while the visiting backs were fairly well fed, the home men in the same position, had little to do, save to tackle and stop rushes. An irresistible rush, headed by Thorn- ley, Ashton, and Davies, gave considerable trouble to the home defence. Pendlebury relieved by kicking to Jolley, whose kick went to touch near the goal line, and from a long and quick throw out by Rowe, Jolley got a grand try under the posts, which Heesom converted. This early reverse completely staggered the home team, and for a time they had all the worst of the game. Jolley took a pass from his opposing centre and threw to Thornley, who was only pulled down under the posts, From the succeeding pack, however, a spell of pretty passing between Rowe, Mather, and Webster resulted in the last named dashing his opponents at one side and getting a fine try. The home team now put forth stren- uous efforts to break away, and ultimately succeeded in dribbling to their opponents' quarter, when Heesom grandly saved the rush. Then came a very fine piece of play by Warrington. It was started by Rowe, who got from a pack finely, and the ball was passed through the hands of Knowles, Mather, and one or two others until it finally reached Oxley, who dashed over the line. For some unexplained reason the try was disallowed. How- ever, Hughes responded to this with a fine run from a line out, and after a very fine display of kicking a tre- mendoue punt by Jolley took play to the line. Warring- ton led at half time by 1-1-4 to nil. Turning round, the game for seine time was of an interesting nature, War- rington in the end being forced back on their lines. A grand screw scrimmage relieved, and headed by Eyre-s, Molyneaux, and Ashton, the visitors transferred the game to midfield. After some more rather monotonous play some very fine passing by Rowe, Mather, Jolley, and Webster ended in the latter dropping at goal, and and Heesom raciar up caught the ball and got a capital try. Runcorn then had the best of the play for a short time, but Boscow by a grand piece of work neutralized. Some capital smart forward play he Oxley, Isherwood, Byres, and Davies gained a lot of ground, but from a fair catch Woods made a good attempt to place a goal. and a minor was shortly afterwards given. A spell of short passing, by llollingworth, Robinson, and Lee was nullified by the grand kicking of the visiting backs, but Dutton, Barker, and Moores eventually dribbled to the line. The stay was of short duration, for a fine dribble, in whi..th Eyres. Oxley, Molyneaux, and Knowles were notable, quickly took the ball out of danger. Im- mediately afterwards Boscow had a kick charged, and the home forwards missed an easy chance, and when time arrived Warrington won by 1-2-4 to 1 minor. Teams :—Warrington Boscow, back; Webster, and Heesom, three-quarters; Mather and Rowe, half backs ; Thornley (captain), Molyneaux, Davies, Ashton, Eyree, Oxley, Knowles, Niold, and Isherwood. forwards. Runcorn : May, back ; Cawley, Woods, and Pendle- bury, three-quarters ; Holfingworth and Robinson, half backs ; Hughes, Stubbs, Lee, Moores, Hulse, Dutton, Williams, Clarke, and Barker, forwards.
WARRINGTON v. DEWSBURY.

The recollections of Dewsbury's visit two se.aions ago was sufficient inducement for a large concourse of people to assemble at Wilderspool on Saturday, when the return match was played. The first g,aMe this season resulted in favour of the Tykes, who secured, it will be agreed, a rather lucky victory, scoring a dropped goal and a try to the Warringtonians two tries. Since that time a marked change has taken.place in the Warrington ranks, and on the play of both clubs being weighed up, public form pointed to the chances of the Laacashire lads. Although the weather was threatening, and rain fell a short time before the match, it happily kept aloof while the game was proceeding. The visitors arrived late, and then only mustered twelve men, three substitutes being found in Tears, Warburtan, and Howarth. When it became known to the spectators that a poor team had been brought by the" shoddy" men, the interest in the match abated, and :there was an entire absence of that excitement which otherwise would have existed. On the home side Nevins was away, and Fair Turner was re- serving his energies for the gymnastic competition which was set down for decision at Liverpool in the evening. A stiff breeze blew from goal to goal, and Massey losing the choice of ends defended the pavilion citadel, Turner starting the game by kicking off to Brook, who ex- changed kicks with Massey, the advantage resting with the visitors. From a line out near the home quarter flag, Gillespie got an opening, but Evans pulled him up near to the line. This surprising form of the visitors was certainly unexpected, and the spectators called for an extra effort from their favourites, but it was no use, Warrington had to adopt defensive tactics. Barnes, however, intercepted a pass from Collier, and dodging oast Gillespie, he raced to Scott, where the oval was transferred to Lawless, but the chance was not taken, and a certain score lost. A long drop at goal sent the oval to Evans, who pluckily ran out, and this movement being seconded by smart dribbling on the part of the brothers Dillon and Handles, the visiting 25 was reached. A mark by Lawless aided his side little, for the effort was promptly neutralized by a spell of passing by the Tykes, a final kick by Brook sending the oval in touch near the Warrington line, a minor eventually accruing. Immedia- tely on the restart Gillespie looked like scoring and Forrest almost struggled in, but Massey, intercepting a pass, raced away, and was not content until he had punted in touch near the Dewsbury line. Some smart passing by Antrobus and Bate further improved War- rington's position, when Massey forced a minor after some judicious kicking. A similar point fall to Dews- bury on the drop out; Brook sending the oval into touch- ' in-goal from the half-way flag. Soon after the drop out Donohue came away from a scrimmage at the home quarter flag, and smart play by Collier saved his side at a critical juncture. Teare and Collier each put in a couple of long kicks, and a third minor was credited to the visitors. The Tykes now showed signs of fatigue and the game, which had been of an exceptionally fast nature, was taken direct to the Tykes' quarter, where Massey tried hard to get in. Scott luckily got the oval away, and the Dewsbury forwards passed well, but Handles proved too much for them, and he 'ant away, but again a sorry exhibition was made of the final pass. Povey and Berry showed up with useful dribbles, and Antrobus and Barnes were loudly applauded for a spell of exchange passing. The climax was reached iinmedia- telv after, for Lawless kicked across to his companion wing three-quarter. Massey took- the oval in grand style, and soon placed the issue beyond doubt, and a fine effort resulted in a try, Frank Turner failing at the place. Turner responded to the drop out, and then a grand run by Handles took/the leather over the line, and another try was credited to the Warringtonians, Barnes this time making no mistake with the place kick. Massey met the kick off with a huge punt, and although the visitors seemed to rally, it was to no purpose, for the combined play of the homesters relieved the home sop- porters of anxiety, and Barnes, Bate, Evans, Massey, and Antrobus showing up with individual run, no ad- dition was made to the score, and half-time was called— Warrington, one goal, one try, one minor ; Dewsbury, three minors. The hopes of the Yorkshiremen vvere now very remote, for Warrinkten had the aid of the strong wind, and from the kick off the ball was worked direct to the Dewsbury line, the home forwards missing a rare chance in the first minute. Lawless being pressed sent the oval dead. Massey responaed to the drop out, and Brook replying Barnes was seen making his mark. The kick was well followed up by Massey, and Scott hein:T at fault, a rare chance of scoring was missed, another opportunity of scoring a tangible point being mulled a minute latter. However, after a minor had been credited to the Warringtonians. Evans put in a grand run and kick to the line, and the Warringtonian custodian had hard lines for a score. From the pack which followed in the line, the oval was quickly in the hands of Bate, who feigned to pa.ss, and

the Visitors being baffled, this clover player succeeded in scoring near the corner, the kick at goal being again at fault. From the restart some fine running and passing between Lawless, Bate, Barnes, and Antrobus resulted in Massey scoring his second try, Barnes this time placing the goal.. No sooner had the game been restarted than Hastings was to be seen working his way with the oval at his toes through the Dewsbury defence, and a brilliant try was the result, Barnes' kick at goal hitting the posts. This rapid scoring—three tries in five minutes—com- pletely broke down the defence of the Yorkshiremen, and passing between Bate. Antrobus, and Barnes once more ~took play near the pavilion goal. Scott got the oval away, only to find Littlewood, Donohue, and Massey rushing the oval back, and finally Berry crossed the line, the point being overruled. A fine screw kick by Barnes' from a drop out was well taken by Massty, and then another forward movement by the Warringtonians re- sulted in a fourth minor. This was followed by E. Dillon scoring, the result of some grand dribbling, and from the difficult place Frank Turner placed a goal. On the call of time Barnes had a rare chance afforded him, but his drop went outside the posts, a 'minor only accruing. The whistle brought a one-sided game to a close with the score—Warrington 3-3-7; Dewsbury, 0-0-3 Had Dewsbury brought their full strength the proba- bility is that the issue would have been the same, though the score might not have been so large. The Tykes were out-played 45 minutes out of the 70 contested, and had Warrington taken all the opportunities put in their way, a record must have been established. Individually Massey, Randle, and Evans were the pick of War- rington. •

Teams :—Warrington: Evans, back; Lawless, Barnes, and Massey, three-quarters; Bate and Antrobus, half backs ;F. Turner, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, Bandies, Berry, Oonohue, Littlewood, Povey, and Hastings. Dewsbury: Scott, back; Brook, Gillespie, and Humphreys, three- quarters; Forrest and Collier, halfbacks; Wolstenhulme, Grundy, Haigh, Riley, Squires, Woolman, Teare, War- burton, and Howarth. Referee : Mr. E. W. Flowers, Broughton. WEST LANCASHIRE RUGBY LEAGUE. WARRINGTON V. LEIGH.

Warrington atoned for a defeat on Monday evening, when in the return engagement with Leigh they suc- ceeded in reversing the first meeting of this season, when Leigh proved victorious by two goals to nil. As the first match was played at Warrington the chances were that Leigh would confirm their previous victory by again lowering the Warringtonians' colours, the match being played on their own ground. Warrington were placed at a distinct disadvantage, having to play without several members who have helped to form that combination which has been so consistent in the present year. Credit must be given those who officiated in their stead, for the Brothers Jolley and Rowe surprised even themselves with their all-round excellent play. Leigh mustered strongly for the occasion, and although a cold wind prevailed, some five thousand people turned out to witness the contest.

It was 8.20 when Frank Turner set the ball in motion, and his kick being well followed up by J. Jolley, Smith's endeavours to reply were frustrated. Further ground was gained by a long kick by T. Jolley, and Warrington, despite the fact that they were playing against a strong wind, had the better of the opening exchanges. Coop saved his side grandly at a critical moment, but a move- ment in which T. Jolley and Massey were prominent once more harrassed the home defence. Coop again was the saviour of his side, and his kick being well backed up by the home forwards, Evans found relief by conceding a minor. From the drop-out play was again at the home quarters, where from a line out T. Jolley got away, and a good run to Coop saw the game on the Leigh line. Strive as the Leigh men would, they could not clear, and from some quick passing by the visitors J. Jolley made a fine pass to Bandies, who got in under the pests, the point being disallowed for some unaccountable reason. Free kicks to Leigh were the only means by which they could make ground, but Warrington playing with remarkablee dash and excellent combination at once pressed th, homesters back, and line work by Rowe, Bate. Barnes and Massey almost ended in a score. The Warrington forwards were playing a fine game, and although much less than their opponents in point of physique, their good scrimmaging powers and grand following up served them to advantage, and by this means they frustrated all the endeavours of Leigh to break through their defence. Rowe ran and dodged well, and T. Jolley held Coop near the line. A lucky kick by the home custodian brought timely relief to his side, but Berry and Littlewood each , with individual runs once more placed their side on the I aggressive. Dent dribbled well to Evans, and T. Jolley kicked well to Pendlebury, a splendid piece of work by Barnes preventing a reply. Coop was responsible for the visitors beating a hasty retreat, and then a fine run and pass by J. Jolley to Massey saw the last-named run- ning and punting to the open, but the Warringtonians in their endeavour to score mulled the chance, and a golden opportunity was lost. Shovelton got the oval away from the line, and eventually another minor was recorded. Withonly five minutes toplay, and against such a strong wind, the chances of Warrington were of a rosy descrip- tion, but all doubts as to the ultimate issue of the game were thrown aside when Warrington worked the oval in grand style to near the home line, and after Bandies Dillon, and Barnes had put in somesterling work, a com- bined rush of the Warrington fotwards took the leather over, and Littlewood succeeded in ccuing a try, Frank Turner failing at the place. This point was recivedwith loud cheers, and half-time arriving, the score stood— Warriagton 0-1-0- Leigh 0-0-2. With the aid of the wind Warrington made matters at the recommencementpretty lively for Leigh. Worthington started by tricky play, but kicks by Evans and T. Jolley sent the oval to Coop, who took the leather in neat style; but Barnes, Judging his man aecurately, brought him to grass betore he could clear. Determined play by the visiting for- wards compelled Coop to kick dead, another minor fol- lowing immediately after, the result of a strong forward rush. Leigh were busily kept defending, until Gregory and Worthington got away, and Evans saved in daring style. McMaster, who was now figuring at back, was compelled to defend his char.ge, and although he was sorely pressed he got the oval away time after time when the greatest odds seemed against him. A fine run by Pendlebury was neutralized by J. Jolley, and his effort being supplemented by another run by his brother, the Leigh quarters saw play being contested. Leigh narrowly missed scoring from some loose play, and only the judicious kicking of Bate and Rowe prevented the disaster. A fair catch to Massey took the game tp the half way flag, and Coop was again forced to kick dead. Smart dribbling by Dillon, Donoghue, and Povey nega- tived an effort by Worthington, and although the last- named got away immediately after, the safe tackling of Barnes prevented his travelling far. Minors fell in quick succession to Warrington, and a minute from the call of time Barnes had a shot at goal, the ball going about a foot outside. On the call of time Warrington had won a hard fought game by one try and six minors to two minors.

The Warringtonians are to be complimented on their sterling all-round play, and there is not a single instance where we can point to weakness. Each man strove hard for the victory they so gallantly achieved, and to make a distinction as to the merits of any individual player would be an injustice. Teams —Warrington:: Evans, back; Massey, T. Jolley, and Barnes, three-quarters ; Bate and Rowe, half backs ;F. Turner, Randles, Povey, E. Dillon, W. Dillon, ,Berry, J. Jolley, Donoghue, and Littlewood, forwards. Leigh: Coop, back; Worthington, Smith, and Pendle- bury, three-quarters; Shoveltnn and Dent, half backs; Lawson, Gregory, S. Pendlebury, R. Taylor, J. Taylor, Glynn, McMaster, and Langford, forwards. Referee, Mr. F. A. Grover, Swinton.

At Detroit, on Monday, Alexander Cuddy, an old man of over sixty, having reason to suspect the fidelity of his wife, a younr, woman not half his age, attacked her with an axe, beat out her brains, and then committed suicide.

Mr. Henry Heady, brewer, of Daynton, Gloucester- shire, met with his death by falling into a vat of beer at his brewery, it is supposed while skimming off the berm. He was not missed for some hours after the occurrence.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 10, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 10, 1890

THE NATIONAL GYMNASTIC CHAM- PIONSHIP. FINAL COMPETITION AT LIVERPOOL. The final tie for the Challenge Shield and Milton shields, offered for competition by the National Physical Recreation Society, was decided at the Liverpool Gymnasium, on Saturday. Although there was a large •audience present, the building was not crowded. Many of those present accom- panied the team from Warrington, among these Warringtonians being Mr. Thomas Morris, Alderman Sutton, Mr. Daniel Joites, Mr. James Smethurst, Dr. Peacocke, Mr W. Dimelow, Mr. W. C. Baines, Mr. G. F. F. White, Mr. Spinks, Mr. John Evans, Mr. John Hesketh, and Mr. H. 11. Kvans (lion. secretary). The judges were the Rev. E. F. Crosse (Bedford Leigh), and Mr., C. M. Roberts (director, Ancoats Gymnasium), while' Lieutenant-Colonel G. Coates (Chester Garrison) officiated as referee. The com- peting teams were Dundee, who had beaten Hud- dersfield, Leeds, and Dublin ; Liverpool, who had previously disposed of Newport and Aberdeen; and Warrington, who had met and vanquished Exeter Hall (London), Bournemouth, and Sefton Hall teams. Mr. J. J Evans, C.C. (chairman of the Liverpool Gym- nasium), presided, and was supported by Mr. fhaanenr GrAnsaoxic, M.P. (president of the National Physical Recreation Society), who, in an intro- ductory speech, observed that the society had of late grown very considerably. Its success had exceeded the anticipations of those who started it. In consequence, a great responsibility devolved upon its managers and upon the members of the Council. In view of those cir- cumstances he might mention that the Council had re- ceived a very considerable number of complaints, and it was with special reference t& those complaints that he wished to say one or two words. The complaints had referred in the main to two points. First of all they had been made against the judges who had been engaged in adjudicating at the various competitions for the na- tional and district shields. He would say at once,on be- half of the Council, that if any member of the society could suggest to them anything practical in the way of Improving the present system of the appointment of judges, those suggestions would receive the Council's best consideration. (Applause.) But he must take that opportunity of making a most earnest and emphatic protest against the practice which seemed to be gaining ground, not only with regard to gymnastics. but to athletics generally, of expressing dissatisfaction with the actions and decisions of judges. (Hear, hear.) It was not easy to get judges to officiate. They had a very difficult and arduous task to perform, and it must be remembered that gentlemen engaged in judging gymnastics had an especially difficult duty, because the judging was to a certain extent a matter of opinion, and it could not be founded altogether upon definite results as in the case of football and cricket. That being so, the spectators should be careful in their criticism of judges who volunteered to give their ser- vices, at considerable trouble and expense to themselves, impartially and with the sincere object of doing a public good. (Hear, hear.) The Council were very careful in their selection of judges. They selected experts;: men who were thoroughly competent for the work; and of whose impartiality they were practically certain. In the second place, he wished to say that the Council would on all occasions support to the utmost of their power the position and the decision of judges, who con- sented to act as such. • (Applause.) Proteste have been made against the choice of the localities in, which, com- petitions had taken place. The Council had recently received a protest against the selection of: Liverpool on the present occasion, becausd it was alleged, the sym- pathies of the audience would be naturally,,for the most part, in favour of Liverpool, and the expression of those sympathies might influence the judges. (" No no.")' Not a bit of it. (Hear, • hear.) He quite agreed, with that gentleman. (Applause.) Athletics pursued in a proper spirit and proper system were altogether good. It seemed to him that, in connection with football„ the players as well as the spectators were eqtially to blame;. the spec•ators were hoping to see something barbarous, hoping to see brutalities in the game, and were there- fore, very often inure to blame than the players were. (Hear, hear, and cries of "No, no" and "Shame.") As representing the Council of the National Physical Recrea- tion Society, which was endeavouring to promote athle- tics whereever it could—athletics of all kinds—he said they ought all to use their influence to create a better spirit, to ensure that those manly games should be played in an English and a manly spirit—(applause),--and he hoped that the members of the society would on all occasions Jo their utmost to see that games were con- ducted in a fair, operwand manly spirit. (Hear, hear.). Credit was due to the Liverpool and Dundee for having undertaken the extension of the society's work in their districts. The Warrington gymnasium—(cheers)—had grown up and developed with surprising rapidity, and he congratulated the members on the success with which they had met. (Applause.) ' The competition was then proceeded with. Liverpool were the first to enter the arena, the initial perf nenance ' being a combined display of barbell exercises. The Liverpudlians are a fine muscular set of athletes, and made a capital show, going through the different move- ments with a rhythm and regularity which were remark.. able. Warrington followed with a highly commendable performance, which told of careful coaching,. and persistent, painstaking practice, but lacked the clockwork swing and movement of the Liverpool men. The chiels from o'er the border came marching in to the appropriate air of "Bonnie Dundee." One of the items, which took immensely with the audi- ence, was a figure from the Highland Fling, The judges, however, did not take the same view of the per- formance as the majority of the spectators, and, out of a possible 98, awarded Liverpool 93, Warrington 84, and Dundee only 80. The announcement of the figures was,. notwithstanning Mr. Qladstone's preparatory injunction„ received with loud cries of dissent. The marks, it should be remarked, were awarded for "precision, grace, and beneficial" movements., and the argument urged in support of the judge's decision, in the case of Dundee, was that their -exercises, though "taking." and showy enough, were not of a ..,eneficial order. Voluntury exercises on the parallel bars came next. Dobson made an indifferent start for Liverpool, A. Vernon- did little better for Warrington, but the dissatisfaction.' which was expressed at the treatment of Dundee in the bar-bells was intensified by the award of only 4imarks to Kinnison for his parallel bars performance. After this every competitor went to work with a will, and put 1 in all he knew. The Warrington men did not dna& well on the bars as might have been expected Only twoof I the team reached double figures, whereas seven of the' Liverpool and five of 'the Dundee men obtained ten or more marks. John Hulmes slipped in starting and, although he tried hard to make up for it, was unable to get more than five marks. His. brother, despite a bad l-eg,inning, managed to obtain nine. Of the other members of the tea in Fairfield Turner, who met with an encouraging reception, madd 8 marks. Cr: Vernon fell two :behind his Sefton Hall form, gaining only eight marks as against ten on his last public performance. Warren vexhibited a decided all-round improvement, which it was a pleasure to witness.,. Locker and Podmore did the best for their team in this department, each getting ten marks. 'rhe aggregate totals for the bar exercises were Liverpool 84, Dundee 75i,. and Warring- ton 67, Dundee thus dislodging Warrington from second ' place and having q points in. hand. The high jump was the succeeding item. In this con- test Liverpool lost the services of Day,, who wa,esuffering from a sprained ankle. Despite this abstention the team, who are particularly strong in this branch of athletics, beat their opponents with comparative ease, the average of the seven c.mpetitors being nearly /0i- out of a maxi- mum of 12. The Warrington average, fora full team, was a little over eiAlit. The jumps were made over a lath which, for a start, was placed at *ft. 21n.,, a comfortable hop for an ordinary athlete; yet, at 4ft. Yin. Locker was out of form in this part of the competition, and soon had to confess himself beaten, but this is fully accounted for by the fact that the accident that prevented him taking part against Sefton Hall, at the circus, also prevented him prac- tisine•''' for the jump. Hence he very naturally fell back in form Podinore and Warren carried off chief honours among the Warrington representatives, each obtaining full marks. James Holmes cleared only 4ft. 9in., which is 2in. below his Circus record. Fair Turner, instead of repeating if not improving upon his last performande, fell hack to his Bdurnemouth form, and accounted for 41t. only. John Holmes also was a point behind his old register. The two Vernon s man- fully tackled an extra inch and topped it. Dundee made
a miserable beginning, one of their men failing to get over the first mark. In the result Liverpool finished eight points ahead of Warrington, and Warrington two in front of the Scotehmen.

The concluding competition was hand-over hand rope climbing, and all the members of the Warrington team, with the exception of Warren, beat past performances. Liverpool finished with an aggregate for the whole corn- petition of 303 i ; Warrington totalled 268 i. The Scotch- men taiiiited the rope-climbing with rare spirit ond pluck, and as a result it will .be seen that they finished just four points ahead of Warriqgton thus winning second place. Total far Exercises The Liverpool team thus become tbe holders of the 200- guineas challenge shield, each of 'the" eight," with their instructor (Mr. A. Alexander), receiving a " Milton " shield in repousse silver, valued at 0-b. The reward of the Dundee men consisted of a bronze shield (valued at £5) emblematic of "Fame," one going to each member of the team and their instructor (M}: A. Sturrock). The premier shields are of gilt end oxidized, framed in plush velvet. The subject is taken from Milton's " Paradise Lost," and the original is entirely hand wrought in repeusse chasing. It is considered to be one of the finest examples of chasing ever made in ancient or modern art. It was acquired by the Government 'at a cost of £2,000, and placed in the South Kensington Museum, London. The nine bronze plaques which the DLITICIVI9 men carried off are framed in plush velvet, and represent " Fame " riding through the air on a winged horses. holding in her hand the scroll of fame, and surrounde by a halo of light. At the conclusion of the competition;. the Chairman said he was proud as a Liverpool man to,frild that Liver- pool had won the challenge shield—(Cheers)—but he hoped the losers would not be discouraged. (Hear, hear.) Warrington, he understood, were, quite a new chib, and must, therefore, be congratulated upon making such a good display. (Cheers.) The competitors from Scotland also deserved hearty congratulation on their success. (Applause.) The shields were then formally presented CO the win- Alava, and the proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the Chairman and cheers for, the winning teams.

The match between the West Lancashire •League win- ners (Wigan) and the Rost of the League ended on Wednesday, in a win for Wigan by one goal, and two tries, to one goal, one try, and three minors. The "Rest of the League" was, however, not a very representative team, as it did net include a, player from either Warrington or Widnes, and wa.s mainly made up of the twa clubs of Tyldeslev and Leigh. Afterthe game the Mayor of Wigan presented the local teaut with the West Lancashire League trophy, which ,it must be acknowledged on all sides has been very fairly won.

Warrington made another step forward in the League competition on Monday, when they defeated Leigh on their own ground. One the most unexpected reverses of Warrington in the early stages of the competition was inflicted by Leigh on the 'Vfilderspool ground, sothat it may be said, after the game of Monday, that the two teams can cry quits. The victory was all the mere creditable to Warrington seeing that they hadso largely to call upon their second string men to make up their teem.

It is to be hoped for their own ci edit that the Dews- bury organisation do not often send out such a weak and disjointed team as they sent to Warrington on Saturday. To fulfil one of their fixtures with a team ,which is alto- gether short of three players, for whom substitutes had to be found. and which contains scarcely any of their best known players, is a tax on the patience of the club with which they enter into engagements. Under the circumstances Warrington did the best thingty" rubbing it in" as they did. They might have rubbed it in a little more if`they had tried.

The St. Fielens Recs. appeared on their own ground for the last time this season on Saturday last, when they met and administered a severe defeat to the Castleford team. The last seasan has teen a successful one so far as the Recs. club is concerned—though perhaps, in the averages it does not compare favourably with last season's record.

Up to and includinz last aturday's engagement the Ree, have played 37 matches against some of the lead- ing organisations in the North of Etu,dand, during the tast seven months. Of these 24 have been, won, 10 lost, and there were three drawn games. The glassmakers ran up the big aggregate scoring of 4r'goalh,, 63 tries,and 122 miners, while their opponents have notched 14 goals, 28 tries, and 77 minors.

In individual brilliance " Jimmy"—Pllkington, who recently secured county honours, has been to the fore, and during the season lie has obtained, no less than 31 tries. " Jacky " Ellison, another popular player, is next on the list wit l 18 tries, while Jack: Seddon proved suc- cessful in twelve attempts to "drop?" goals.

VOOTBALL—ASSOCIACTOff. The Earlestown team accomplished a smart perform- ance, on Saturday last, when they lowered the colours of West Manchester, on the latter's ground. It was the re- turn League fixture between the two dabs, and Earles- town deserves every credit fel the, manner in which they defeated their more celebrated' opponents.

RUSSIAN. TOUR BY THE GERMAN
EMPEROR.

A St. Petersburg correSpondent hears that the Emperor William has written to the Czar requesting permission to make a tour right through Russia. The German Em- peror's request will, of course, be granted. It is believed the tour will be down the Volga and the Caspian. and perhaps as far as Central Asia.
THE EIGHT HOURS MOVEXIENT.

The societies affiliated to the London Trades Council have resolved. to invite the London districts tO declare in favourof an eight hours working day without anystipula don as to the method by which such eight hours shall be obtained. It has further been decided not to demonstrate on therst of May, but to do so on the first Sunday in May, as the most convenient time. .

div.head: NEW GERMAN CHANCELLOR,
div.p: NEW GERMAN CHANCELLOR,

General' Caprivi made his first .official speech in tbe Prussian PArliament on Tuesday. The Chancellor said that the coarse of the ship of State would remain the same, and he declared that he would co-operate with all who desired to foster a Monarchical spirit nv Prussia and a national spirit in the Empire. The Chancellor's decla- ration was very 'warmly received. A step which has also been taken towards the suppression of the " semi- official " press- has also given much satisfactran.

div.head: BONDON TRAGEDY.
div.p: A BONDON TRAGEDY.

The inquest relative to the death of M. Albert de Giedon, who on Fiiday shot himself at the'llotel de l'Europe, London, after wounding, a girl with whom he had been living, was'opened on Tuesday, and adjoui necT for a week. The girl',..who is the daughter of M. van Mussiel, of Liege, has•made a statemerA to the police to the effect that De ' Giedon placed travelling trunks against the door of the'açartmont, asked her to swear that she would never forsake him, and then shot her, in- flicting serious injuries:. The young man had previously offered to introduce her to his friends in Paris, and stated that he would marry her.

div.head: DEATH Or AN MISR
div.p: DEATH Or AN MISR

Mr. Matthew Harris,.rnember for East Galway since 1885, died on Monday evening, near Ballinasloe, from cancer in the stomach w Mr. Harris was origina ly a bricklayer, and subsequently a builder and contractor. He was an advanced Nationalist, and oneof the members involved in the "charges and allegations" At a. meeting of the Irish Parliamentary party on Wednesday, in the House of Commons, Mr. Parnell pre- siding, a resolution was adopted deploring the death of Mr. Matthew Harris, M.P. for East Galway, and express- ing sorrow that he had net been spared to enjoy the victory of the Irish people in their national struggle.

div.head: MURDER I k LONDON BAKERY.
div.p: MURDER I k LONDON BAKERY.

The murder of a bread picker, named Thomas Furlon- ger, at Messrs. Nevill's bakery, Mullwood-road. Herne Hill, London, is causing much excitement at that place. The deceased was found in one of the furnace rooms on Saturday, dead, having been killed with an iron bar and robbed of his week swages. It is asserted that a man has made a statement practically ameuntinr, to a confession of the crime, and that the motive was rob- bery. • An inquest was opened at Herne Hill, on Tues- day evening. Daniel Gderie, a fellow-workmen of deceased, is under remand on suspicion of murder. The inquest was aajourned until the 29th inst.

div.head: INTE' MYSTERY.
div.p: THE INTE' MYSTERY.
INQUEST ANT) VERDICT.

The inquiry relative to•the death of the two little girls who have been missing from their home at Bird-st., Ince, since the 31st ult., was held on Monday, at the Walms- ley Arms Hotel, Ince, before Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner. Both children, Selina Humphreys and Janie Holland, reeded with their parents in Bird-st., Ince. On the 31st ult. they were missed from their home. Every inquiry was made without success, until Saturday morning, when the former was discovered floating in the canal. The child Holland was found .a few yards distant in the earns lock, on Sunday morning. The parents, who were much affected, gave evidence of identification. Ellen Stott gave evidence as to the children being toge- ther on the 31st ult.—Dr. Drayton stated that he had made a post-mortem examination of both children. The children were well-nourished and healthy, and there were no marks of violence. The cause of death was suffocation from drowning.—A Verdict of Found drowned" was returned.

An article was published in the "National Zeitung," on Tuesday, contradicting some of the statements Mr. Stanley is represented to have -made in an interview at Brindisi, with regard to the relief of Emin Pasha and the position in which he was found. The writer makes his statements on the authority of Emin himself, who is, he says, the most modest and sincere man imaginable. TIPPOO TIB AND THE GERMANS.

The Berlin correspondent of the " Daily News" tele- graphs that according to adviees from Brussels, Tippoo Tib has asked permission of the Congo Government, and received it, to leave for Zanzibar. The "Vossische Zeitung " concludes from this statement that Germany will try to avail herself of his services for the expedition under Ethin Pasha to the interior. It may, be remembered that.some time ago rumours of negotiations between Major Wissmann and Tippoo Tib's son were circulated.

div.head: MR: sr ANLEY AT CANNES.
div.p: MR: sr ANLEY AT CANNES.

•Mr. H. M. Stanley arrived at Cannes at half-past eleven on Saturday. He was received at the station by Mr. John Taylar,tite British vice-consul, and Sir William Mackinnon, cliairnsian of the Emin Relief Committee. In accordance with the wish of the Prince of Wales, Mr. Stanley proceeded immediately to the Hotel of his Royal Highness. After having, an interview with the Prince, he returned to the Hotel Continental, and was engaged all the afternoon, upon his new bAk. In the evening he dined at the hotel with Sir William Mackinnon and the, delegates of the,F,ast Africa Society.

div.head: THE, RAILWAY RATES INQUIRY.
div.p: THE, RAILWAY RATES INQUIRY.
LOCAL EVIDENCE,

The proceedings in connection withthe Board of Trivie inquiry as to railway rates and charges under the Rail- way and Canal Traffic Act, 1888,;. were resumed on Monday morning. The inquiry was now specially directed to the question of the classification of gocialls. The neat subject which gave rise to discusqion: was the classification of alkalies. Dr.. Hewitt, of Brunner, Mond, and Company, of Winnington, near Northwich, said thatthe traffic in articles under this head ainsonted to something like 1,300,000 tons ci year, and the ntherests at stake. were therefore considerable. These articles were at present carried in a special class of the. Clear- ing Muse classification. With, some exceptions they were carried in large quantities and it was the fault of theerailway companies that they were not carried in ail huge quantities as pig iron. The reasons was that the railway companies ha di not given such great facilities. The traders ciirotended that MI quanti- ties: over four tons ought tee be put in a lower class a charges than they were at present. He specially mentioned bleaching powd4rsulphate of ansmonia, and carbonate of soda. Quantities of from five to ten tons iought to be reduced to the' lower class B, and the traders were perfectly willing that the articles should be con- signed at the owner's risk..—Mr. Wilkinscn, for the rail- I t way companies, arguedittiat the high value of some 05' the articles under this head, and the care required ia :handling them, clearly entitled the railway to higher !rates than those undeeciass B.

A claim was made by sweral repzesentatives of *a tanners' industry, tot have fleshings and the pieces re- duced to class B. It was stated that the matter Waaot great importance to tanners throughwt the countrv,and that large quantitieswere consigned by the different rail, way companies to Liverpool for shipment. The railway companies opposedany reduction irtthe rates on amount of the unpleasant nature of the traffic. A claim was made to put gra4l in class B instead of the higher class, and claims were also made in favour of placing a mini- her of other articles in the lower class, after Which the inquiry was adjOurned until Tuesday. The Committee of the Warrington traders en- gaged in the tanning trade were represented at the inquiry by Councillors J. H. Fleming and William Pierpoint who were in attendance at London on Monday and Tuesday. Mr. Fleming's evidence chiefly related to the trade in green hides and that of Mr. Pier- point to dry hides. Both gentlemen supported the con- tention of Mr. Lafone, M.P., who represented the tanners of thecountrv, that high railway rates would have a very prejudicial effect upon the trade in these two classes of hides, not only locally but throughout thecountry gener- ally.

div.head: PROPOSED INFIRMARY ExTENSION AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE PROPOSED INFIRMARY ExTEN- SION AT WARRINGTON.

On Monday morning a meeting was held at the Town Hall, Warrington, in connection with the proposed. extension of the Infirmary, and for the purpose of taking stepsto raise the necessary funds. Alderman, Davies was elected to preside, in the absence of;Mr; J. C. Parr (president of the Infir- teary and Dispensary Committee). There were also present—The Revs. S. Wilkinson and Father Feeney; Major Pickmere, Major Litton, Captain Withingtent and Captain Tuckton, Dr: Starkey Smith, Dr. Gar' nail, Dr. Richmond ; and. Messrs. William Owen, r• Monks, 11, Broadbent, George Dakin, Alfred Woods, Joseph Tvriss, G. Legge, William Sharp, T. Cawley, John Roberts, John Shepherd, John Taylor, and J• H. Waring, Ake Workingmen's Committee of the Infirmary being represented by Messrs. John Roberts, 111, Waring, G. Legge, and Taylor. Messrs. Joseph Davies and J. Lavercock Tunstall were Pre- sent as joint honorary secretaries of the InfirmarY. • The CHAIRMAN, .in the coarse of his remarks, said he held lb his hand the annual report of the Dispensary the year 1820; from which he found that although War: rington was a town then only with a population Of 15,000, that the great and noble fellows of that day sPeet as much as-£.400 a year in. providing a Dispensary for the poor of the town. (Applause.) He referred to the poor who were not chargeable to the parish. In theyear 1863,whertle jeinea the institution, and became seer& tary, they were in the unenviable condition of having £l5 in hand to carry on at the end of the year, and theY also owed £54 which they could not pay. They had, it was true, £lOO in the Savings' Bank, which the late Mr. Parr had given them; in 1863, and they were at such a low ebb that they had to spend it, and even then they owed £lo2elos. 3d. Twelve- months' credit had been given for repairs.. But, he was thankful to state, War- rington had not been behindhand since 1863, and at the present time they had a funded property of something like £15,000 or £16,000; a building which cost from £8,400 to £9,000; and that was a state of things which in a gre it measure had been brought about by the efforts of the working-men of Warrington. Those who were better off were now called upon t, give their help, and he had no doukt they would liberally subscribe to sun' plement whatthe workinganen of Warrington had se nobly done. They could not carry out the proposed ea' tension unless they had an increased income. There was a large amount of sickness in the town which could be better treated by an exteneion of the building, and it vcas - owing to the suggestion made by the hon. medical offi-• cers of the institution that the extension was to be made. He thought the inhabitants of Warrington generallY should give freely to enable the enlargement Ls be effected. (Hear, hear.), The CHAIRMAN then explained a plan of proposed alter- ations„the plan having been prepared by Mr. W. Owen. One of the wards, he remarked, was to be called "The Beamont Ward," in memory of the first Mayor of War- , rington, a gentleman who during many years had Wl' dered valuable service on behalf of the institution. . would be 'situated oven-the Hatton Ward. In the uPPer storey woutd be the operating-room, which would be a befr ter room for the purpose than that which was now used. The present Dispensazy would be utilised for more bet% and the new Dispensary would be built at the rear of the Infirmary on land to be granted by the Corporation. He was happy to be able to inform the meeting that before they had an opporturity of sending out alt appeal for subscriptions, he - received a letter from Lord • Winmarleigh, who said' he heard that it was intended to increase the accommodation of the IntirmarY and Dispensary, . and that the sum of £3,00 would be required for thee purpose. If £2,500 of that cold' be raised he w.oald contribute £5OO. (Applause.) He had had great pleasure in waiting upon Mrs' Peamont, who, with great propriety, was anxious to contribute towards. the extension, but she wished to d° something not counected with "The Beamont Ward." She had announced her intention to give {Applause.) , Alderman Davies also announced other contributions,„aalist of which is given below. A Sub' scription had also. been promised by Mr. Carson on be: kalf of the Whiteeress Corapany. He (Alderman Davies) had called tosee-Sir A. B. Walker, but found that gentle' man from, home, as he had been called away oil very urgent business. He would no doubt be able to see, bins later on.. (Applause.) Mr..Wriazalit OWEN explained that the present number of beds at the Infirmary was 23; when the extension Was' completed,39 beds would be provided. (Applause.) Councillor,F. Moues said he hoped the result of thee meetingwhichliad been held that morning would be,' losuccessful. He had ventured to suggest to ma. John Roberts. (chairman of the Working-men's Committee)' that if that Conunittee could raise £5OO, the enlargement' of the institution could be carried out without datficultl• or trouble., (pear, hear.) Mr'..Joun,l3namars said that since 1880; the working- rnen.of the town had contributed the handsome sum, of about £l,OllO towards the funds of the Infirmarl- (Applause.) He was not authorised to mention any Sum- buhe thought his Committee would be able to raise £6.so°' (Aal/lause•) Mr, W. SHARP moved" That it is highly desirable tbat_,,' tke.extensions and alteratina of the Infirmary, propos°s'. by the Board of Management, be carried into effect, and that separate funds be established into which subscrie- tons may be paid respe,etively for the I3eatnont wAri :and for the general purposes of the Extension Coin? imitbee." He did not think there votild be any troublo in raising the whole amount recmired, and that with" out resorting to a bazaar, which they had been, threat- ened with. (Laughtor). Bazaars were ,esod thing a• us, their way, but in a case like the present he believed thee' was no necessity to hold one. (Hear, hear)i D. STARKEY SAME seconded the resolution.whieis• unanimously carried, The CHAIRMAN said that the amounts which had been promised were as follows :—Lord Winmarleigh, £5.00 Mrs. Beamont, £l0; Messrs. Monks' Hall, and. C„<nn; pally, £lOO ; Mr., Sharp, £5; Mr. Robert DavieSa „ Mr. Joseph Davies, £5O : Mr. Naylor, £50.; and Mr. s' H. Blackly, £sot. div.p: A ROMANTIC SUICIDE.

. • . According to a despallch from Cologne, the bodies ef a rithly-dressed lady, about 32 years of age, and a well- dressed young gentleman, apparently not more than 23 Years old, have been found in the Rhine near that city, ted together round the waist and the neck with shawls and towels. The couple were doubtless lovers who had "solved to die together. Nothing which would be likely to lead to identification was found on the bodies. THE ATHERTON MURDER.
EXECUTION OF WILLIAM CHADWICK.

_ On Tuesday morning, at eight o'clock, Wm. Chadwick 'was executed at Kirkdale Goal, for the murder of W. 'Bayles, pawnbroker's assistant, Atherton, on the 22nd JulYi 1889. Berry was the executioner. The weather was cold and damp, but this did not deter a small num- ber of people from assembling near the goal to witness the hoisting of the black tag. The condemned man as pinioned in the corricjpr of the prisoner's reception- uouse. He submitted very quietly to the operation, giving Berry no trouble whatever and making no com- Plaint. As soon as all was read!, the Under Sherriff (Mr. Wright) gave the signal to move on, and the pro- cession, if it could be called so, went to the scaffold in the old coachhouse; which was only a few yards distant from the pinioning corridor. In the procession were the governor (Major Knox) and the Rev. D. F. Pigott, the chaplain, who was reciting the Litany for the Dying (not the Burial Service of the Church, of England, as is customary on these occasions). Closely following the Prisoner was Berry, the executioner, who was dressed and got up as he was an the occasion of Richard Davies, at linutaford. He had the same striking headgear, camely, a Turkish fez. Chadwick just before the e•aecutioner left him, and after the cap had been drawn, turned towards Berry and apparently whispered leraething to him.. Berry at once gave the informed( n ~ge was seeking. Chadwick turned aswell as he could Lo the chaplain, who was standing alittle in the rear, and said in a very distinct voice to him, "Give my love to 11/ dear wife." Then he turned towards some of the gaol officials, who he knew were standing close to him, although he did not see them, in consequence of the cap cg over his face, and said, in resonant tones, "Good- ye, and the Lord bless you." The Chaplain, who was tieeply affected, replied "Good-bye:; God bless you, my ta4l." Berry then moved to the lever, and touching the andle the trap-door opened and the body fell into the Pit. Death must have been instantaneous. Chadwick, during the morning, behaved with calm- -85 and in a manner becoming his dreadfnl position. Suite a friendship seemed to have sprung up between iin and his spiritual adviser, to whose ministrations the convict listened with willingness. Chadwida, how- ever, on Tuesday morning, as belies •done all along, as- ted his innocence of the charge for which he suffered the death penalty. He acknowledged himself to be a thief, but he denied that he was a murderer. On Mon- day he made a long written statement with reference to .." ra crime. This doeument was handed to the Governor, °Y whom it will be forwarded to the Home Secretary, Major Knox refusing in the meantime to divulge the 'contents or to give any inkling of the nature of the document. The usual inquest was held, and thecustomary verdict returned. TILE DROWNING OF TWO ;WOMEN AT

div.head: MOORE.
div.p: MOORE.

On Saturday morning, at the Ring o'Bells Inn, l'aresbury, an inquest was heldiby Mr. Worsley, as to the death of Mrs. Ana Maria Buckner (65), wife 2,f Henry Buckner, gamekeeper to Sir Richard Isrooke. and Miss Mary Massey (62), lately residing With ber brother, Thomas Massey, wire manufac- turer, of Pendleton, Manchester, arta 'formerly laundry- °laid In the service of Sir ,Qnbert Greenall, 'which en- on Wednesday night last. EVIDENCE OF THE DBLATIVI3S.

Henry Buckner, gamelceeper, Daresbury, said his wife Was 65 Years of age. He last saw her alive on Wednes- 'lay afternoon, the 9th just,, about two o'clock, when she told him she was going to Warrington. As she did hotreturn he became anxious as to .her safety, and ,Shortly before twelve o'clock went out and searched for Oer as far as Moore but could neither.see.nor hear any- thing of her. At that time it wasraining heavily, and the night was very dark. She was familiar with the way along the canal bank, as she had walked-it, many times Previously., she having lived in Dareabury for about two Yeats. Witness, however, considered the place a danger- (xis one, and said he could not see the water two yards from him, even with the aid of a lantern. :It looked like the towing path.—Susannah Phillips deposed that Miss Massey had come over the previous Saturday on a visit tn her, at Daresbury. Deceased formerly lived at Walton Ilan, as a laundress. On Wednesday :morning last she left the village to go to Warrington, and was expected to return in the evening. Deceased told witness,that she Was going to visit some relatives-in -Warrington. As she did not return at the usual time, she concluded that ' 4:leceased had stayed with her friends :for the night.— omas Massey said he was brother .of deceased, and 'Tied at Langton-st., Pendleton., Manchester. He was a brass and wire manufacturer. Previous :to his sister ' e-otning to Daresbury she had been -staying .with him. 'When not in service she always lived at his-house.

, Jesie Lane, aa-tionmaster at Daresbury, said that on the night in question both of the deceased got off.the 'I%4E train from Warringtoen, which arrived at Daresbury 41: few minutes late. He was conversing with them for Out five minutes. Mrs. Buckner had 'a parcel or two With her. They were sober when they left the station. J. L. Jones said he was landlord ofthe Red Lion Inn at Moore. On the night in question the deceased women called at his house about five Or ten minutes past 'tight o'clock. Mrs. Buckner had a. carpet bag in her Possession, containing groceries. Each of them had a glass of whiskey, but they were perfectly sober hen they left the house at half-past eight. Ho gave 13uckner a half pint bottle of whiskey., as a present I.et her husband, whom she had stated WAS unwell. About "vomainutes after the decased left they returned and 464, ed :for a lamp, as it wan very dark. The glass pro- ,`,Uced,was exactly similar to the one belonging to the amp he lent them. Witness asked the deeeasedwhether 4.7 should send his startle boy to accompany them, but that:they could manage to And ikeir way. DISCOVERY OF THE BOMBS, . .

- Vfltiamflastup said he was captain of the canal boat ,"otoria, from Runcorn. He found the bodies Coating tl the Bridgewater Canal on the other side of geckwick ?..iidge, at ten minutes to six o'clock on Thursday morn-. Theymere about 200 yards apart. The current Altnninglin the direction of Keckwick. A Juryman 481 K ed if it was necessary for the bodies to be kept in the ;water tuntil=the police came. In this case they remained 21 the waterthreehours before the police officer arrived. 'neve being plenty of willing hands to take them out in • the meanwhile.—The Coroner said it was a question order. It was safest for the bodies not "" be removed until the police had seen them.— Jackson,.of Preston Brook, deposed to being pre sent when the ,bodies were recovered. In Mrs. Buckner's Pocket he found., in addition to other articles, 12s. 2td. 1 in money, and two half-pint bottles of whisky. There , *ere no marks of 'violence on the bodies.—P.C. Barter, (4 Higher Waite; corroborated. THE VERDICT. , After consiclexation the jury returned a verdict of Pound drowned:"—The Coroner said the question now ose whether anything could be done to prevent these owning accidents oecurring in future. He had visited Lne place that morning, and considered that it was exceptionally dangerous, and there certainly ought to be a Protection of some description. He had expected to see Vinebody representing the Ship Canal Company present, they must remember that the Canal Company were _Perfectly right in using the towing path as a wharf, and 'ore not bound to fence it off. At the same time, a pre- :refitment could be made to them.—Several jurymen 'nonght the place where the accident hsd occurred was very dangerous one, and said the water was also very ,eeP.—Ultimately the Coroner, on the recommendation ho jury, promised to write to the Ship Canal autho- -1!_"55 to see whether sonwthing could not be done to pro- rct the approach trom the road to the footpath leading 142 the station, in view of the number of accidents, some which had resulted fatally, which had occurred at 'oat place.

div.head: iLttters to tbt Obitor.
div.p: iLttters to tbt Obitor.
NORTH-WEST WARD ELECTION.

Sir,—l trust that the working-men electors of the North-West Ward will mind what they are about during the coming week. The Tories are doing all they can to get Mr. John Roberts in. They think the best way to pay him the debt they owe him for doing all he can for Toryism is to get him into the Council for a Liberal ward, but it won't do. Let them find room for him, if they want him, in a Tory ward. Ido trust that the voters will not allow themselves to be humbugged by supposing that John Roberts is anything but a Tory candidate, which means Tory privileges and Tory ex- clusiveness, in other words, everything for the classes and nothing for the masses. Let every voter go to the poll as if the election depended upon him, and then the Tory candidate will get such a " licking " as will make him for ever fight shy of THE NORTH-WEST WARD.
WATER CHARGES LIVERPOOL v. WARRINGTON.

Sir,—Thanks for the insertion of my letterof April 3rd. Respecting your comments thereon, I am perfectly con- tented to leave the matter to the judgment of your readers, the object having been obtained that caused me to address you. In concluding thiscorrespondence, might I suggest the advisability of the formation of a Vigilance Committee, to look after the interests of the ratepayers in the pur- chase of the Waterworks? A committee of this charac- ter would be of the greatest service in elucidating facts and figures, to say nothing of logic. As money would be required for the necessary expenses of the committee, I for one am prepared to stand my equal share to the ex- tent of a £lO note.—Yours sincerely,

div.head: THOMAS GREAVES. 30, South-road, Waterloo, near Liverpool. April 17th. 1890.
div.p: THOMAS GREAVES. 30, South-road, Waterloo, near Liverpool. April 17th. 1890.
RUNCORN CHARITIES, &c.

Sir,—Having read, in the columns of your valued paper, much about our local charities, the writer was drawn to add further to his knowledge by putting in an' appearance at the adjourned vestry meeting held in the Bethesda Lecture Hall; but after patiently sitting through re-appointments to the various ecclesiastical offices for the year, which occupied most of the evening, the worthy Vicar requested all persons present, not being in "regular attendance" at the Parish Church to with- draw, presumably that certain matters, including Charity accounts, might be discussed en camera. Of course those who have read the atcwint, as furnished by your paper, know what afterwards rook place. The few Nonconformists who left the building, in obedience to the Vicar's dictum, seemed to lack leadership—the gentle- men who have lately brought these matters to the fore, showing their profound interest in the administration of the Charity funds by conspicuously absenting themselves on what may be termed the " crucial occasion." However, I must not complain, we are moving in the right direction •, and next year, in addition to the vestry meeting being held in the place "legally appointed," our courteous vicar may extend his usefulness by causing the whole of the accounts to be read ore tellies, imitating the respected Vicar of Halton, his parishioners benefiting thereby. I cannot help thinking that the church "as by law established "is far in advance, in these matters, of our Non-conformist, say the Wesleyans in particular, whose church members are wholly in the dark respecting the business of the church, financial or otherwise. The church government of this latter body is In the highest degree Conservative—" having power to preserve (John- son), and to retain for own use (writer),—and the rank and file, including members holding minor offices, are ignorant of the minds of their "governors." I trust that the "prying snirit " abroad may extend it influence over churches outside the "pale of the law,' and lead their law-givers and administrators to place more ccnfidence in their members and allow them to have a voice in the management of the funds which they (the members) supply, also to remember that "taxation without representation is tyranny."—Yours sincerely, A WESLEYAN MEMBER.

div.head: CHURCH DECORATIONS, Src.
div.p: CHURCH DECORATIONS, Src.

Sir,—Our Parish Magazine' Banner of Faith" for this month says Christ Himself is really present as God and man at every Christian altar. This magazine is circulated with (as he calls himself, Protestant) Bishop Jayne's knowledge. Such teaching is downright popery. What is the use of a service for Ascension Day if Christ is at every Church altar? The last rubric in the Communion Office says something different, and Article four tells me He ascended up to heaven, and when He comes again it will be to judge all men. Bishop Fraser said—' 'I cannot say that I apprbve of the elaborate decorations of our churches." Bishop Ryle says, "I very much doubt whereunto these decorations of churches will grow." The present Archbishop of Dublin has recently condemnNi the eastward position, the cross on the communion table, and auricular confes- sion. The dilemma for church decorators is, do they wish their work to be looked at and admired, or do they not? If not, why put it where it must attract the eye ? Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the Lord. But unto Cain and his offering He had not respect. Mr. Gladstone says "There are few things more honour- able than to be defeated in a good cause." My cause is -sound truth, and I intend to peg at it. ROBERT FOULKES. Frodshani, April 18th, 1890.

div.head: ROMAN CATHOLIC ON "MORE FACTS."
div.p: A ROMAN CATHOLIC ON "MORE FACTS."

Sir,—l do not take up my pen to write you a long history of facts in contradiction to the letter by "- Dis- senter" which appeared in your issue of the 12th inst., but discussions on the various questions ot religion have ever been and still are matters of inevitable necessity; because Christianity has ever been,and still is, impugned by those victims 6f passion, prejudice, and error, the schismatic heretic and infidel. If illfeelings are some- times engendered by these discussions, the fault lies with those who first. raise the standard of rebellion against the teaching of the lawful pastors, whom Christ corn mis- sioned to feed His lambs and His sheep with the bread of life and the word of God. To elucidate truth is my object, and, as a Catholic reader of your valuable paper, I cannot help noticing the prejudice that still exists in the hearts of such men as" Dissenter" and his Foulkes brethern. Catholics as regards doctrines court publicity, because they are fully aware that the *more these are tried and examined the stronger will be the conviction of their truth in the mind of she sincere inquirer. Now and again a letter appears in the columns of your valu- able paper from such men denouncing Catholics as lepers, or demons let loose from the pits, and never tells the truth about Catholic beliefs. Your correspondent advises a trip t 6 Normandy to see " Catholicism" in its unadulterated state. Now, I would advise your readers not to spend their hard-earned money in going such a long journey in order to See the very same thine. which is carried out at the pres-nt time in any Catholic'"Charch in England ; the same doctrine, the same ceremonies, and the same beliefs. lie states that no mention is made of Christ (as in England) a statement which is a downright, villanous lie ;and, again, that rank Mariolatry prevails. Nsw I was speaking to a person not long ago who was in Brittany recentiveand he was giving me an outline of how fervent Catholics were in that part of the globe (something like the Irish) who maintained and upheld the old established way of serving God which was once the custom in this dear land of ours. To explain the truth about the Catholics' belief about the Blessed Virgin would take too long in a letter, but I cannot help noticing the gradual revival (with satisfaction) of the devotion in honour of " Mary " the Mother of God, in nearly all the churches in protest- ant England ; and I may add that to my mind a few years (considering the hundreds of conversions which have taken place recently)will suffice to see all England, her sons and daughters,t rue and obedient children of that 1 Church which once made her a *nation.

Your correspondent doesnot like the saints, sym tols, or the smell of incense, evidently, and sneers at them because he does not understand what they mean; but it was as well he went to the nearest Catholic priest'or la,y7
man who would give him the desired information. But why does not he tell the truth about indulgences? Any one reading his letter can penetrate his bigotry, and even

if his compagne de voyage was so shocked at all she saw it was very easy to make her astonished ; and your cor- respondent does not tell us whether it was at the grandeur of the ceremonies or at the error of her ways. He winds up by appealing to your numerous readers to study " Macaulay's History" (with a biased mind). Let me also ask your readers' kind indulgence to suggest that they read not alone Macaulay', and every Other history written by any other man either Catholic or Protestant, and study the Bible, and get at the true meaning of the word of God and they will thep feel satisfied that they 61 are right,—if they do this unbiased and boldly dare to act upon the Protestant principle of examining for them- selves.

In conclusion, I may. now add that I am exceedingly pleased that everywhere throughout the land tolerance at present reigns, signs of the ref urn of the lost sheep appear, crosses and rases are presented and accepted for use in Runcorn Parish Church, and Frodstfam is coming to the front in trying to Show how, by making use of flowers, first, the parishioners thereby give external expression to the interior sentiments of' respect, devo- tion, and religion; secondly to enliven and increase devotion and piety, by moving and striking the senses; , thirdly to lead the simple and illiterate more easily to a knowledge of the mY•steries of religion. And even if they do this, Mr. Editor, there is not so much harm, after all, ! in these wicked Papists, such as your humble servant, i • THOMAS WILLIAMSON.

div.head: EXAMINER; SATURDAY, APRTL 19, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER; SATURDAY, APRTL 19, 1890.
PENKETH. THE ,POOR RATE.
At the Warrington, County Petty Sessions, on Wednesdayf a poor rate of one shilling in the pound for the township of Penketh was signed.
THe LIBERAL CLUB.

The ammo/ meeting of the Penketh Liberal Club was held in the clubroom, Penketh, on Monday. There was a fair attendance of members, the following being amongst those present :—Mr.J.T.Gummersall,president Messrs. C. E Parker, A.J. White, F. Hughes (secre'Ary). W. Longthaw, R. Garnett, Ames Davies, J. Mainley, Routletlo J. Hayes, .Tame A. Wilkinson, W. flayes;.,George Bates, S. Griffiths, T. Seed. J. Simpson, J. T. Budden. W. T. Wilkingon, F. Goulden, &c. The officers for 1889-90 formally resigned, and the chairman, Mr. j. T. Gummersall opened the proceedings by a criticisrd and review of the balance sheet. It was grati- fying tp him to note that for thefirst time in three veers, there ,was. a balance to the goodrnannely,. £4 4s. 11d.; last year the balance was £3 as. 2d. on the other side, so that the gross surplus on the yeafe work just passed would be £1 7s. lid. There wag a falling off in the amount of members subscription, wltoh wagattributable to some members beineconslderablYin.arrearg. Although 0, balance was brought forward to the credit of this year's work, the club was still largely in,debt, owing to loans— which are still unpaid—en the purchase of the new Hard table. A discussion took place with regard to the building of a Public Hall. The progress of the cause in Penketh is hampered by there being- no suitabl* room in which to ventilate questions of importance. The chairman thought that the people in Penketh were behind the times. They were between two large towns, the village was fast rising, and soon more roam would be wanted; and peaple would be wakened up upon the subject of politics. The club had done a work in the way of prorMing recreation far the young men, but he thought more might be done in this direction ,and also wished theyeouldinfasealittliernere spirit in actual politieal work.—Mr. C. E. Parker, in speaking-on the question of a public building, said he would be glad to help the movement on. A room' was very badly wanted were-questions upon any subject could be freely discussed. At present they were handicapped in this direction. end he hoped that efforts would be made to remove this difficulty—Some discussien here took plate in which Mr. H. Garnett. Mr. W. Loneshaw, Mr. A.. 1. White, and T. Seed took part. A vote-of thanks to the officers for the past year was accorcitel;.and the follow- ing were re-elected :—Mr. J. T. Gumersall, president ; Nice-Presidents. Messrs. C. E. Parker, T. H. Bolton, R. Harnett, J.Peers, D. Garnett, H. Hughes; G. Broadhurst; Trea.surer, Mr. A. J. White; Secretary. Mr. F. Hughes ; assistant, A. Grenhalgh. A committee of eight members' was also appointed.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
MINSTREL ENTERTAINMENT AT THELWALL.

The Warrington Amateur Minstrels gave a miscellane- ous entertainment in the Coffee Room at Thelwall, on Tuesday evening, in aid of the fund which is being raised to take the scholars attending the Ship Chnal (No. District) School for a day's trip to the seaside. There was a good attendance, the programme coneisting of comic and sentimental songs and duets, stump speeches, humorous sketches, banjo eccentricities, and cornet solo, the whole forming a most enjoyable entertainment.

div.head: ANOTHER " DUG-der " UNE LRTHED:
div.p: ANOTHER " DUG-der " UNE LRTHED:

Another " dug-ont canoe, has been found in the course of excavation on the klanchester ShiP, Canal.. It is very similar in size. and appearance to that discovered at Barton about twelve months ago, and in quiteas good preservation. rile site- of the new discovery was at Partington, not far from the confluence of the Mersey- and the Irwell.

div.head: SALT SPRING DISCOVERED.
div.p: SALT SPRING DISCOVERED.

A brine spring has been discovered in the cutting of the Manchester Ship Canal near Partington. The water from the spring is being tested in order to ascertain its strength and the probable richness of the assumed salt beds. If the result is satisfactory, boring will no doubt be resorted to. Shoeld it be proved that rich deposits of salt underlie the company's property, the importance of the discovery to the company, not only as regards the development of a salt industry, but also with respect to traffic on the canal, is manifest,
SINGULAR DEATH IN A COLLIERY.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquiry, on Wednesday, at Ashton, relative to the death of Wm. Jackson, fifty-nine years of age, of 65, Edge- green, Golborne. The evidence showed that the de- ceased was a furnace man, employed by the Oars- wood Hall Colliery Company, at their No. 5 pit. On Sunday afternoon last he was at work in the mine. He came up from the mine about three o'clock in the after- noon, and after staying up a short time, he was let down to, the bottom. He ought to have signalled to the engine man on arrival, but failed to do • so. About five o'clock, a collier named Beaman wanted to go down, and Top- ping told him to signal the deceased. He knocked several times, but got no answer, and then it was thought something unusual had occurred. Bea- man was let down the shaft in the other cage, and on getting to the bottom he searched for the deceased, and ' found him in the dib hole, partly under the cage that Beaman had descended in. He was quite dead.—All the witnesses agreed that it was probable that in conse- quence of the cage having been let down very slo4ly by the winder the deceased had made a mistake, and that he had stepped on to the " bonnet," thinking he had arrived at the bottom, and then had slipped off and fall-- en into the position described.—The Coroner having summed up, the jury found that death was due to the injuries, but how caused they were unable to say.

div.head: DISTRICT CONVENTION OF GOOD TEM PLA RS.
div.p: DISTRICT CONVENTION OF GOOD TEM PLA RS.

The Tio. 1 Convention of South-west Lancashire Good Templars met in the Primitive Methodist Tabernacle, Ashton-in-Makerfleld, on Saturda afternoon. Bro. Col.-Sergeant Devlin, C.C.T., of Warrington, presided, and .there was a large attend- ance of represeatatives from Earlestown, Warring ton, Golborne, &c. Among the visitors present werr Bro. J. Pickersgill, of Liverpool, Bro. T. Williams (Widnes), and Bro. and Sister Sutherland (Illhdlev). The monthly reports were submitted; and were of a favourable character. It was arranged that the next session should be held under the auspices of the Ebenezer lodge at St. Helens. Bro. Sutherland, of Hindley, gave a brief address, and Bro. J.Pickersgill, D.E.S.,in the course of a paper on "Beware of Strong Drink," urged the adoption of steps for increasing the membership and use- fulness of the order. He asked them as Good Templars to exercise their votes and influence in a direction that would tend to lessen the power of the drink traffic, and to vote only for those candidates who would be pre- pared to support temperance measures if elected to Par- liament. A discussion followed, in which Bro. J. Vint, Sister E. Clarke, and Brothers G. E. Warburton, Geo. Clarke, T. Beaton, J. Taylor, T. Frain, &c., took part. A vote of thanks was accorded to Bro. Pickersgill for his paper. A tea meeting was afterwards held, and was largely attended. Bro. S. Spruce,C.T., of Ashton, occupied the chair, and gave an address. A programme of songs, recitations, readings, &c., was rendered by Sister Sutherland (Hindley), Bro George E. Warbuqon (Earles- town), Bro. J. Taylor (Earlestown), Bro. Sutherland (Hindley), Sister A. Devlin (Warrington), Sister A. Whittle (Haydock.), and Bro. Geo. Clarke (Earlestown). Bro. W. Whittle' of Ashton, was the accompanist. An address on the benefits of Good Templary was given by Bro. J. Pickersgill, DES., of Liverpool, and the meeting terminated with a vote of thanks to the entertainers, &c.

There was a good attendance, including Mr. Peter Stub's (in the chair), Mr. and Mrs. T. P. Norris, Mr. W. Ilattersby, and Messrs. H. Saville, E. Gibbons, Marsh, Thomas Ardern, A. W.
